News.title: Labour’s £3bn contract crackdown will hit pubs, care homes and youth jobs, bosses warn
News.content:
LABOUR’S crackdown on zero-hours contracts could cost business up to £3 billion, a damning government assessment reveals.

The party came to power with a pledge to ban “exploitative” zero-hours contracts as part of a new workers’ rights package.



But top bosses last night slammed the rising cost of taking on workers and said it will do further damage to the youth inactivity crisis.

The workers’ rights package has been spearheaded by former deputy PM and now Communities Secretary Angela Rayner.



The impact is set to be most concentrated in industries where demand is more variable including hospitality, the arts along with health and social care, government documents show.

Andrew Griffith, Shadow Business Secretary, said: “Labour’s jobs tax and employment red tape have been so damaging already, but this goes further and once again, it will be young people who will pay the price, during a growing crisis of young Brits out of work.”

Firms have had to deal with hikes to national insurance hikes and minimum wage increases adding to the burden on business since Labour came to power.

Kate Shoesmith, from the British Chamber of Commerce, said: “The increased cost to businesses of the proposed changes to zero hours contracts will be a further hammer blow for many firms struggling to keep their heads above water.

“The government had previously claimed that the cost of the entire Employment Rights Act for business would be £1bn but this research clearly blows that out of the water.

“Businesses have seen their costs due to government policy increase by 70 per cent in the last decade, and their ability to absorb more is extremely limited.



“We are already facing a youth unemployment crisis – now is not the time to make it even more costly for employers to hire.

Kate Nicholls, Chair of UKHospitality, said: “The eyewatering cost of these reforms comes at the worst possible time for hospitality businesses, arriving on the heels of more than £5 billion in additional employment costs in the past two years.

“More than 100,000 jobs have already been lost in hospitality as a result and the extraordinarily high cost of employment continues to restrict job opportunities, particularly for young people.”

Workers on zero-hours and low-hours contracts will get the right to guaranteed working hours from next year if they want them.

The government is consulting on whether to apply the policy to anyone working 48 hours a week, but its preference is for the threshold to be between eight and 20 hours.



Firms will also have to fork out if shifts have been cancelled or moved at short notice in a huge financial blow.

In a worst-case scenario, the right to guaranteed hours could cost firms £450 million.

Then the right to reasonable notice of shifts could cost £1.2 billion and the then £1.3 billion for the right to payments for shifts cancelled or moved.

In a best-case scenario, the overall direct cost to business could be £350 million.

No final decisions on what is deemed an exploitative zero hours contract or what reasonable notice should be given. The consultation runs until next week.



The planned reforms will still “support growth” by improving conditions for workers, an impact assessment said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesperson last night said: “We are absolutely committed to ending exploitative zero hours contracts, where workers bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable.

“These reforms will give workers in every postcode greater income security and predictability of hours and while no final decisions have been made, we’re consulting to get the detail right and ensure this works in the real world.”

News.title: What time is the Clacton by-election result? When to expect the winner announcement and full list of candidates
News.content:
CLACTON voters will soon discover who will be their next MP after a record-breaking by-election.

Polling stations open at 7am on Thursday, but the 34-candidate ballot means the count could run later than usual.



What time is the Clacton by-election result?

There is no guaranteed declaration time, but the result is expected before breakfast on Friday.

Reports say the winner should be known in the early hours, while the complicated count could push the announcement back to around 5am.



Once voting ends, ballot boxes from 51 polling stations must reach the count centre.

Officials verify that the number of papers matches the polling-station records before counting all votes.



That job may take longer than normal because Clacton’s ballot paper is almost a metre long.

Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said its record size created practical problems, including how staff would spread the sheets out while allowing candidates’ representatives to watch.

He explained: “Administratively, it’s about how we fit this ballot into the envelopes for postal voters, and – when the voters receive their postal votes – how they get it into an envelope and get it back to us because it is that long.

“We also have an issue for the counters, how we’re going to lay it out, how we’re going to ensure that those who are watching can see while at the same time managing these metre long ballot papers.



No exit poll is planned, so voters should not expect a 10pm projection.

When do polls close in Clacton?

Voting runs from 7am until 10pm on August 13.

The contest uses first past the post, so each elector chooses one candidate and the person with the most votes becomes MP – they don’t need to secure more than 50% of the vote.

The by-election was triggered when Nigel Farage resigned as Clacton’s MP on July 8, 2026.

Farage took 21,225 votes at the 2024 general election, finishing 8,405 ahead of Conservative runner-up Giles Watling.

News.title: Map reveals parts of UK with ZERO asylum seekers as Andy Burnham vows to send migrants to leafy middle-class suburbs
News.content:
MORE than a dozen local authorities house no taxpayer-backed asylum seekers, analysis shows – after Andy Burnham said more middle-class areas should take in migrants.

Our map reveals migrant hotspots across the country, with Glasgow, Hyndbyrn and Blackburn among the places supporting the most asylum seekers per capita.



Mr Burnham yesterday suggested that wealthier areas should take more people into dispersal accommodation.

He told GB News: “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers.”



The PM added: “I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part.”

Mr Burnham was responding to protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, where the village of 350 people held a mock independence referendum over plans to house 1,000 asylum seekers at a MoD base.

Humans rights groups, the local council and MP Calum Miller have objected to the controversial plans for “Site A”.

The list of 17 areas, first compiled by the Daily Mail, shows posh areas like the Derbyshire Dales, the Isle of Wight and the Cotswolds house zero asylum seekers.

Migrants are more likely to be housed in areas with higher deprivation scores, a Government metric used to track poverty.

Areas with high numbers of asylum seekers and a high deprivation score include Burnley, where there are 455 migrants, or 46 for every 10,000 people.



Similar areas include Middlesborough (43 per 10,000), Blackpool (34) and South Tyneside (42).

The asylum seekers are split between emergency accommodation and dispersal accommodation including hotels and HMO properties, Home Office data shows.

The 17 areas with NO asylum seekers Ceredigion, population 72,599 Cotswold, population 91,661 Derbyshire Dales, population 71,757 East Hertfordshire, population 156,875 Hart, population 103,162 Highland, population 237,290 Isle of Wight, population 141,660 Isles of Scilly, population 2,366 Malvern Hills, population 83,227 Mid and East Antrim, population 139,913 Mid Devon, population 84,993 Mid Ulster, population 152,718 Na h-Eileanan Siar, population 26,020 New Forest, population 176,116 Orkney Islands, population 22,020 Shetland Islands, population 23,190 Tewkesbury, population 101,949

This morning, Anna Turley, the immigration minister, defended Mr Burnham’s remarks.

She said: “I think this is about fairness, and we won’t be asking anyone to take more than they can.

“It’s about their fair share, and we have to look across the country at what is appropriate for areas to take, what is the infrastructure, what is manageable with the local community.



“So this is about fairness.”

And pressed on the Piddington development, Ms Turley said: “The reality is, this is a military base that is outside the village. It’s self-contained.

“People there will be managed and processed properly with the services that they need there on site.

“So we are looking to reduce the impact on local communities.”

But Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “Andy Burnham is planning to dish out another vindictive punishment beating to the UK’s middle classes.



“Labour has hammered hard-working families with punitive tax increases galore, increased regulation and soaring energy bills.

“Now, Burnham plans to deliberately flood more neighbourhoods with thousands of illegal immigrants who he has let into this country, and many of whom will commit serious crimes including rape and murder.”

Mr Burnham, who visited Dover for the first time as PM earlier this month, has already seen 3,000 people cross the Channel since July 20.

More than 15,000 have crossed from France this year, lower than in the same point of the last two years.

The tally includes 230 who arrived in a single “mega-dinghy” in the early hours of Monday morning.



Home Office sources insisted that migrant smugglers had only resorted to larger boats as interceptions were increasing.

A spokesman added: “We’re cracking down on these reckless and dangerous gangs – our work to disrupt their criminal supply chains has led to more than 1,100 small boats and engines seized since the election.

“There are also now more police on French beaches to intercept them before they set off.

“Small boat crossings are significantly down this year with the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.”

News.title: What time does Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026? When to check status of university offers
News.content:
STUDENTS will soon find out whether they have secured a place at their preferred university, with A-level results just around the corner.

Thursday, August 12, is results day for hundreds of thousands of teenagers – and for those seeking to remain in education, Ucas plays a big part of proceedings.

What is the difference between A-level results and a Ucas score?

A-level results are the traditional letter grades from A* to E that students receive from your exam boards.



Ucas score, also called tariff points, is a numerical value assigned to those letter grades, allowing universities to compare different types of qualifications equally.



Each letter grade you achieve in a full A-level translates into a specific number of UCAS points:

A*: 56 points

56 points A: 48 points

48 points B: 40 points

40 points C: 32 points

32 points D: 24 points

24 points E: 16 points

Your total Ucas score is calculated by adding the points of all your eligible qualifications together.

Your total Ucas score can also include points from other qualifications outside of your A-levels, such as Extended Project, AS-levels, T-levels, BTECs or music exams.

You can use the official Ucas calculator to total up your projected score.

What time does the Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026?

Students will be able to access their applications from 8am when the embargo is lifted.

Individual records typically process across the system between 8am and 8.15am.

However, with thousands of students logging in simultaneously, expect slow loading and be patient.



Avoid refreshing the page constantly, as this could worsen server traffic.

The Ucas customer experience centre phone lines open at 8.30am if you need direct troubleshooting assistance.

The Ucas Hub tells you where you stand with your firm and insurance university choices.

It will not show your actual grades – those only come from your school or college.

It could show one of the following outcomes:



Your place at your first choice is confirmed

You have been placed at your backup

You have been offered a changed course, which might mean a different course, a different start date or a different point of entry

Your application is still awaiting a decision

You are eligible for Clearing

You then need to check the details of the offer and do what the university asks, which may include proving your qualifications or meeting any outstanding conditions.

A changed-course offer requires a quick decision – you normally have five days to accept or decline, and letting it sit could cost you the place.

Awaiting a decision does not mean you have been rejected.

Universities sometimes take students who have narrowly missed an offer, so it is worth getting on the phone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Students can only use Clearing once their status says they are eligible, or when they have formally declined or released themselves from a place they are holding.



Clearing choices will become available to students from 1pm on results day.

News.title: Co-op lorry driver wins £19k after female colleague accused her of ‘flashing’ her breasts to get ahead at work
News.content:
WORK ROW Co-op lorry driver wins £19k after female colleague accused her of ‘flashing’ her breasts to get ahead at work

A CO-OP lorry driver has won a £19k payout after a female colleague accused her of “flashing” her breasts to get what she wanted.

Charlotte Brooks was left feeling “humiliated” after co-worker Kerry Dawson accused her of performing sexual favours to get her own way.



Miss Dawson told the HGV driver just because she has “tits she thinks she can flash them at anybody and anyone will do anything for her”.

Charlotte said that the “bullying” continued for two years, and Co-op agreed the comments amounted to sexual harassment.



Dawson was sacked, but later successfully appealed against the decision.

It meant she was then able to return to work, leaving her victim anxious and distressed.

Charlotte has now won £19,042 for claims of sexual harassment and direct sex discrimination after suing Co-op.

An employment tribunal held in Exeter, Devon, heard she started working for Co-op on January 17, 2022, as an apprentice lorry driver.

Ms Dawson was an apprentice driver at the same time.

While on a training course in Bristol in July 2022, Ms Dawson alleged to instructors Charlotte would perform oral sex to get what she wanted.



She was “very upset and gutted” when she found out this comment had been made about her.

Charlotte then told her manager about it, but did not want to attend mediation because she thought this would not solve the issue.

She added that there were more instances of bullying from Ms Dawson and that the situation escalated.

In October 2024, she was sent a voice note by Ms Dawson which was later deemed to be “inappropriate” by Co-op bosses.

It said: “Just because she’s got fucking tits she thinks she can flash them at anybody and anyone will do anything for her.”



Charlotte submitted a grievance and it was investigated by Co-op.

The company found that Ms Dawson’s conduct between June 2022 and October 2024 had been “inappropriate”.

During a meeting, disciplinary manager John Rowan said: “You [Ms Dawson] freely admitted during our meeting that what you did was wrong and that you had been stupid in your actions.”

He said that as she had admitted what she had done and the company had a ‘zero-tolerance approach’ to this behaviour, she would be dismissed.

Ms Dawson appealed, and the decision to dismiss her was overturned and replaced with a written warning.



Bruno Krssak, who conducted the appeal, said that there was a ‘historical conflict’ between the two colleagues.

Mr Krssak added that the original decision had been “procedurally flawed”.

The original meeting failed to give Ms Dawson relevant information prior to the hearing and that there was “hearsay evidence”, he claimed.

Charlotte was told that Ms Dawson would be returning to the workplace in January 2025, with no discussion of safeguarding arrangements for her.

After hearing this news, Charlotte became so ‘distressed’ that she signed herself off as unfit for work due to work-related stress.



She then remained off work until February.

Employment Judge Paula Volkmer said that Ms Dawson’s comments amounted to sexual harassment.

She said that the appeal process had not taken into account the seriousness of Ms Dawson’s conduct and the effect on Charlotte.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

EJ Volkmer said there was a “theme of minimising the harassment of a sexual nature”.

She added: “I consider that if the conduct had been between members of the opposite sex, Mr Krssak would have taken it more seriously.”

News.title: Punter wins six-figure scratchcard just two years after landing £1.5m jackpot – & has incredible plans for winnings
News.content:
A LOTTO LUCK Punter wins six-figure scratchcard just two years after landing £1.5m jackpot – & has incredible plans for winnings

A LUCKY punter has defied the odds to become a two-time lottery winner, landing a £74,000 jackpot just two years after scooping £1.5 million.

Cristien Breton, from North Carolina, has revealed his incredible plans over how he’ll spend his second lottery payout after winning on a supermarket scratch card.



The lucky man from Salisbury has committed to putting the £74,000 ($100,000USD) winnings back into the community to help underprivileged children as they prepare for the upcoming school year.

His extraordinary donation comes as he is still yet to spend all of his winnings from back in August 2024, when he won over a million pounds on a $20 scratch card.



He told WCNC this week: “I could not believe it happened again. I’ve been very lucky.

“I want to help take care of the community. It feels awesome. I am definitely blessed.”



Cristien used his first winnings to help support his mother, which he said motivated him to keep paying it forward.

Winning the lottery more than once might seem impossible but it’s actually be done on multiple occasions.



In 2023, a Brit won the £1million lottery jackpot three years after he landed £12,000.

David Lawrence scooped the massive lottery prize win playing the same numbers as he did in 2020.

He said: “We were lucky enough to have won about £12,000 three years ago using his numbers but never in our wildest dreams could we have imagined that these same numbers would lead to a £1,000,000 win.”

It comes as a lottery player who binned an £860 winning ticket managed to retrieve it from a rubbish tip after days of searching.

The unnamed woman threw away her ticket after she was told by a small shop in Bitonto, a town in Southern Italy, that it was “non-payable”.



The woman pleaded with the local rubbish collection company to help her recover it, launching a major search-and-rescue operation to recover her jackpot.

They managed to track down the disposal truck before it dumped the waste into a compactor and stopped it.

News.title: What time do A-level results come out? When to get your grades on results day 2026 and how to collect them
News.content:
HUNDREDS of thousands of teenagers across the UK are bracing for a nerve-racking morning on A-level results day.

Here is all you need to know about what happens on the day, and how to collect your grades.

When do A-level results come out?

This year, A-level results day falls on Thursday, August 13.



The Joint Council for Qualifications sets the date and it applies across every exam board, including AQA, Pearson Edexcel, OCR, WJEC and CCEA in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.



This covers AS Levels, the Extended Project, free-standing maths qualifications, as well as Level 3 applied and vocational technical qualifications.

OCR’s Cambridge Technicals at Level 2 and Level 3 can be issued to students slightly earlier from Monday, August 10, but schools and colleges can choose to hold them back until the main results days.

Exams officers can see results on their systems from 12.01am, but they can only give results slips to students from 8am.



Bear in mind that 8am is the earliest permitted time results can be handed out – not a fixed release time.

Each school or college has its own specific policy on when and how students can collect their results.

How do I collect A-level results?

There are several options available for how you can collect your grades on the results day:

In person: Go to your school or college with your photo ID to collect a printed slip with your results. If you personally cannot attend, give your institution a written letter naming your proxy with their ID to collect your results for you.

Go to your school or college with your photo ID to collect a printed slip with your results. If you personally cannot attend, give your institution a written letter naming your proxy with their ID to collect your results for you. Online: Log into your institution’s online portal to view your grades. Most results are sent to UCAS and your chosen universities or colleges automatically, so you can also use the UCAS Hub to see if your university place is confirmed, but this will not show raw grades.

Log into your institution’s online portal to view your grades. Most results are sent to UCAS and your chosen universities or colleges automatically, so you can also use the UCAS Hub to see if your university place is confirmed, but this will not show raw grades. Email or post: Check your email inbox, including the spam folder, if your institution sends digital copies. Some schools mail physical copies if arranged beforehand.

Schools and colleges set their own arrangements, with some handing out printed slips in person while others use online portals or email, so it is worth checking your specific institution’s policy.



Can you challenge an A-Level grade?

The request to review marking must come from the school or college itself, so you will have to speak to your exams officer should you wish to challenge your grades.

If they refuse to ask for a review, you are entitled to use the school’s internal appeals procedure to challenge that refusal.

A review can push a mark down as well as up, which is why the student has to give written consent and the school has to keep it on file.

There may also be a fee if the grade does not change, so it is a good idea to check what it costs first.

If a university or further education place hangs on the outcome, the cut-off for a priority review is August 20, otherwise the standard deadline is September 24.



When the exam board sends out the result of your review, you have 30 days from that date to appeal it.

An appeal has two stages – if you are unhappy with the first answer, you have another 14 days to ask for a hearing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you have asked for a review that could change your grade, tell the university straight away.

The exam board does not tell Ucas or the university that a review is underway, but it will report any grade change that comes out of it, and the university is under no obligation to hold your place in the meantime.

News.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
News.content:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral
News.content:
Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Burnham considers disposable BBQ ban over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government is considering a ban on disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

Some retailers have already decided to voluntarily stop selling the devices, which have previously attracted warnings from fire chiefs.

A potential ban is being discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures chaired by Burnham.

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

Speaking during a visit to Stevenage, Burnham said a disposable barbecue ban was something the government was "certainly going to consider".

He said he understood why people might want to use the grills outside, but added: "We need to, in my view, have a situation where almost we just have a temporary ban on those things. We're going to look at that issue today.

"I don't know whether we can persuade retailers to do that, but I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear that people should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time.

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

News.title: Jasper Carrott says family is 'so proud' of Lucy Davis after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, who was one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

News.title: PM warned of Iran war impact on UK growth next year
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been warned that the UK economy could barely grow next year if disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues until the end of 2026.

Treasury sources have confirmed that internal modelling presented to the new prime minister and chancellor suggests UK GDP growth could be as low as 0.3% in 2027, as first reported by Bloomberg.

Government officials say they routinely plan for all possible scenarios.

The UK economy saw a strong start to the year, but growth then faltered with the conflict in the Middle East affecting some businesses. The Iran war has pushed up oil and fuel prices, and also disrupted supply chains.

On Thursday, official figures will show how much the economy grew between April and June of this year.

Economists are expecting growth of 0.4% for the three months.

Burnham and Chancellor John Healey were presented with a reasonable worst-case scenario of the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively closed for the next five months, and no permanent US-Iran peace deal until the new year.

The Treasury modelling for that scenario was that the UK economy would grow by 0.9% over 2026 - slightly under the 1.1% forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March.

The prospect was much dimmer for next year, with just 0.3% growth projected - much lower than the OBR's 1.6% forecast for 2027.

Under the modelling, inflation would peak at 4.3% in the first three months of next year. It currently stands at 2.6%, just above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The prime minister and chancellor will face pressure to use the upcoming Budget on 28 October to ease the financial burden on households and businesses.

Since taking office three weeks ago, Burnham has announced policies including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to "subscription traps".

But this week he told the BBC's Wake up to Money the announcements, aimed at tackling the cost of living, are not enough on their own, hinting at further support.

He has asked Healey to look at what more the government can do on the cost of living in the Budget, with the chancellor saying it will be his "main focus".

But Healey has said he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

Burnham has said his government will stick to the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase people's income tax, VAT or National Insurance contributions.

He also promised to follow the fiscal rules imposed by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

News.title: Eurovision Song Contest changes rules for countries at war
News.content:
Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year.

The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna.

It states that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

The update will be interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv.

They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool.

News.title: How the weather will affect your viewing
News.content:
One of the most spectacular solar eclipses the UK has seen for decades is taking place on Wednesday 12 August.

From around 18:00 BST, the Moon will begin moving across the face of the Sun, creating a partial solar eclipse across the UK.

At its peak, around 90% of the Sun will be covered from London. In Cornwall, as much as 95% of the Sun could be obscured.

Depending on where you are in the UK, it will peak between 19:02 and 19:16 BST.

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief inspector warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".

He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.

The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.

News.title: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
News.content:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

News.title: Estonia rejects proposals to take prisoners from UK jails
News.content:
The Estonian government has rejected the idea of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British jails.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a deal signed last week.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.

The Labour government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Pakosta said Estonia had received no proposals to rent its prison space from the UK, adding that if one was to be made "our answer would be unequivocal - in Margaret Thatcher's famous words: No. No. No."

She added: "Such a proposal would not merely be mistaken, misguided or unacceptable; it would deserve to be rejected outright."

Thatcher memorably repeated "no" three times in 1990 speech, as she fiercely rejected calls for deeper political and economic integration of the European Community, which later evolved into the European Union.

In 2024, the Labour government, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, held talks with Estonia to discuss the Baltic state's policy to house some prisoners from abroad.

Pakosta previously told the BBC she had met then-UK Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood in Lithuania.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is planning to release thousands of prisoners early this October, as it scrambles to free up space in jails almost at 100% capacity.

On Monday, Downing Street did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons, when asked by reporters if the government was considering doing so.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government was focused on "creating that extra capacity within the system domestically".

"In terms of renting prison places abroad, it's just not a quick fix," the spokesperson added.

"It will require primary legislation underpinned by a complex international agreement which would take several years to agree."

A government source told the BBC that renting foreign prison space would not help with the short-term crisis in jails.

Burnham has ordered the justice secretary to come up with a plan to create more space in jails by September.

He said the plan would be based on removing more foreign national offenders from prisons, releasing some offenders on indefinite sentences, and using space in women's jails for male inmates.

News.title: Semi-pro footballer filmed driving at 191mph
News.content:
A semi-professional footballer who was filmed driving at 191mph has been jailed.

Connor Charlton, 32, was also involved in a scam where other drivers took penalty points for speeding offences in return for cash, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The centre forward, who plays for Nostell Miners Welfare FC in the Northern Counties East League, was seen in footage drifting his BMW at a roundabout, almost crashing into a van. A passenger also filmed him driving at 191mph on a motorway.

Charlton, from Hunslet, was sentenced on Wednesday at Leeds Crown Court to four years in jail and banned from driving for four years and seven months.

He had admitted 10 counts of dangerous driving and four offences of perverting the course of justice.

News.title: Windermere signs to warn of algae poisoning risk
News.content:
Dozens of signs warning people about the dangers of algae poisoning are to be placed around England's largest lake.

About 40 notice boards alerting visitors to blue-green algae blooms, which can produce toxins that make humans ill and be fatal to pets, will be installed at Windermere, in the Lake District.

Blooms occur naturally but are more frequent during warm, dry weather and are exacerbated by nutrients from phosphate in pollutants such as sewage.

Funded by the Environment Agency (EA), a further 40 signs will be placed at other locations across Cumbria.

The Love Windermere Partnership, which includes organisations such as the EA, Lake District National Park Authority and United Utilities, said it was installing the permanent signs in response to requests for "clearer and more consistent public information".

As well as explaining what blue-green algae looks like, the notices will provide guidance on where to find current information about blooms and how to report suspected sightings using the Bloomin' Algae app, external.

The microscopic organisms can look like blue-green paint, scum or greenish-brown discolouration.

News.title: Serious failings found in new military crimes unit, leaked report finds
News.content:
A leaked Ministry of Defence (MoD) report, obtained by the BBC, has highlighted serious failings in a new military command set up to investigate the most severe crimes, including rape and sexual assault.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) was launched after the death of 19-year-old Gunner Jaysley Beck. An inquest found the Army's mishandling of sexual assault and harassment complaints made by Beck contributed to her taking her own life, and exposed "systemic failings".

However, an internal review highlighted ongoing concerns with the unit and warned the military still risks failing victims.

The MoD said the findings had been accepted and significant work has been undertaken since.

The DSCC was created in 2022 to investigate serious crimes independently, outside the military's chain of command.

However, the BBC can reveal that an internal review, which was carried out between 21 August 2025 and 12 November 2025 and overseen by a former senior civilian police officer, concluded that if the DSCC was subjected to scrutiny similar to civilian police forces there would be "a significant risk of (it) being graded as inadequate".

In a statement, the MoD said the review was commissioned "to provide honest challenge, identify areas of improvement and to help ensure the highest standards for victims and witnesses".

It added that following the findings, the DSCC had carried out significant work "including further investment in victim and witness support, strengthening governance and safeguarding arrangements and accrediting investigators to nationally recognised policing standards".

The DSCC was committed to transparency, continuous improvement and ensuring victims receive the support and service they deserve, the statement continued.

News.title: Man, 102, in critical condition after alleged pub assault
News.content:
A 102-year-old man is in a critical condition after allegedly being assaulted at a pub.

Emergency services were called to The Crow's Nest pub in Cwmbran, Torfaen, at about 22:25 BST on 1 August, and the man was taken to hospital.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, and has since been released under investigation.

Gwent Police is appealing for witnesses and want to speak to anyone who was in the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 on the night of the incident.

News.title: Family almost miss £1m lotto win after ignoring calls
News.content:
A family almost missed out on a Â£1m lottery jackpot after unknowingly ignoring calls and emails notifying them that they had won.

Builder Mark Jefferson from Ilminster, Somerset, ignored the National Lottery's notifications for nine days before reluctantly answering the phone.

Jefferson, his wife and their four children set up the syndicate in July 2025 to celebrate his birthday.

"Knowing the family has opportunities we have never imagined before is the best feeling in the world," Jefferson said.

The family syndicate matched five main numbers and the Bonus Ball in the lottery draw on 24 June.

Jefferson's daughter, Alexandra, chose the winning numbers.

Eurovision Song Contest organisers have updated the competition's regulations for 2027, declaring that any victorious broadcaster will “automatically be ineligible to host” should their nation be involved in an “armed conflict” or a “sensitive geopolitical situation”.

The update follows boycott threats ahead of the 2026 event in Vienna, where several countries, including Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland and Slovenia, demanded Israel's exclusion due to the war in Gaza. Those nations ultimately did not participate in the most recent contest in May.

According to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the decision stems from consultations with participating broadcasters and aims to offer increased certainty for performers and production teams.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said: “The Eurovision Song Contest is constantly evolving, and our annual review of the Rules is an important part of making sure the contest remains fair, transparent and consistent for all those who participate, including the millions who engage with the event globally.

Bulgaria is due to host next year’s competition following Dara’s victory in May ( PA )

“Guided, as always, by feedback from our members, we have clarified and strengthened several areas for 2027. These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special.”

Bulgaria is set to host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest following the victory of singer Dara at the event in Vienna, Austria, in May.

Israel has finished second in the last two contests, meaning they came very close to earning hosting rights.

In 2025, Yuval Raphael took the runner-up spot with New Day Will Rise, as he finished behind Austrian singer JJ.

Earlier this year, Noam Bettan secured second place for Israel with his song Michelle.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has continued to compete in the Eurovision Song Contest following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Just three months after the invasion, Ukraine won Eurovision for just the third time thanks to Kalush Orchestra’s popular hit Stefania.

Ukraine went on to finish third in the 2024 contest, but have failed to challenge for victory in the last two years, finishing ninth in 2025 and 2026.

Barcelona are yet to agree a fee with Manchester City to sign Rodri as their attempts to bring in Spain’s World Cup-winning captain continues.

The Spanish champions had an initial bid of £38.4m rejected by City last week and have been considering a second offer.

But they are yet to meet City’s asking price, with the FA Cup winners thought to want around £60m to sell the Ballon d’Or winner.

Rodri has entered the last year of his contract at the Etihad Stadium and is keen to return to Spain after seven years in Manchester.

Real Madrid were also interested in the former Atletico Madrid player before Barcelona emerged as the favourites to get him.

City, who have broken their transfer record to sign one midfielder this summer, after paying Nottingham Forest £116m for Elliot Anderson, are considering buying again as they may have to replace Rodri.

They are interested in Morocco’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, while Enzo Fernandez, who played for Enzo Maresca at Chelsea, has an admirer in their new manager.

World Cup champion and Golden Ball winner Rodri also underwent minor surgery on his back following the conclusion of the tournament which makes him a doubt for the start of the new season.

City boss, Maresca, is hopeful that the midfielder will see out the rest of his contract and be available for the upcoming season but City will not want to let Rodri leave for free next summer and they are willing to negotiate with Barcelona for a fair price.

The world’s most powerful and polarising politician will inevitably attract threats from his opponents. Donald Trump has faced several credible assassination plots since returning to office, partly triggered by a more aggressive foreign policy approach in his second term.

Just this week it emerged that the US leader was smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck to escape an Iranian assassination threat when he visited the Nato summit in Ankara last month.

Trump has faced several attempts on his life within his own country too, including during his election campaign in 2024 and during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in April this year.

Below we look at all the credible threats the president has faced from foreign-affiliated actors.

open image in gallery Catering carts reportedly used to smuggle Trump onto another plane ( AP )

‘Money is not an issue’: Afghan man recruited to find hit squad to kill Trump

In 2024, Farhad Shakeri, an Afghan national and Iranian government operative, was accused of hiring two New Yorkers he met in prison to carry out an assassination plot against a critic of the Iranian regime amid rising tensions between the US and Tehran.

While in detention, he admitted to FBI agents that he’d also been recruited to find a hit squad to kill the then president-elect Trump. He was charged over the alleged plot in November 2024.

The former New York resident claimed he was asked by regime officials in September 2024 to “put aside his other efforts... and focus on surveilling, and, ultimately, assassinating, former President of the United States, Donald J. Trump,” according to a criminal complaint presented in a Manhattan federal court.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has been subject to several assassination plots ( AFP/Getty )

Shakeri countered that the scheme would cost a “huge” amount of money, to which his regime contact replied, “[W]e have already spent a lot of money .. . [s]o the money’s not an issue.” He claimed he was given a deadline of mid-October.

In January, Carlisle Rivera – one of the New Yorkers recruited by Shakeri – was sentenced to 15 years in prison for the plot to murder US citizen of Iranian origin Masih Alinejad, a journalist, author, and human rights activist.

open image in gallery US-Iranian journalist Masih Alinejad was the subject of an assassination attempt that also targeted Trump ( AFP/Getty )

“I’m just a woman,” Alinejad said after the sentencing. “My weapon is my voice. My weapon is my social media.”

Jonathan Loadholt, 37, was sentenced to 10 years in March this year.

Iranian spokesperson Esmail Baghaei dismissed the reports at the time alleging they were part of an Israeli-linked plot to disrupt talks between the US and Tehran.

In April this year, Pete Hegseth claimed that the US had killed an Iranian official linked to the assassination plot but did not name the person.

Trump threatens to ‘obliterate Iran’ amid reports of assassination plots

There were reports of Iranian plots last year too, with the US leader saying he had instructed his administration to destroy Iran if it happened.

“If they did that they would be obliterated,” Trump told reporters when asked about the threats. “I’ve left instructions if they do it, they get obliterated, there won’t be anything left.”

He reiterated his instructions in July this year, saying that “if anything happens” he has told his government to “literally bomb them at levels they’ve never seen before”.

Business owner hired by IRGC caught by FBI staging killing on napkin

Trump had another close call when Pakistani business owner Asif Merchant admitted he had attempted to hire hitmen to assassinate the US leader.

He told a US court that he planned to initiate the assassination during the 2024 presidential campaign but American investigators disrupted the plot before it could succeed.

open image in gallery Pakistani business owner Asif Merchant admitted to trying to hire hitmen to assassinate Trump ( Department of Justice )

Merchant said he was carrying out instructions from a contact in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). He said that his handler never mentioned a specific target but broached names including Trump who was a candidate at the time, then-president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.

He was captured after using objects on a napkin to depict a shooting at a rally to an acquaintance but was instead introduced to undercover FBI agents who had secretly been recording him.

The Iranian government has denied trying to kill U.S. officials.

“This man landed on American soil hoping to kill President Trump — instead, he was met with the might of American law enforcement,” U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi said in a statement released after the conviction.

The news came days after US-Israeli strikes on Iran that sparked the current conflict.

Trump hides in catering truck amid Israeli reports of assassination plot

The latest incident occurred during last month’s Nato summit in Ankara.

It came after reports during that same month that Israeli officials had uncovered an Iranian plot to kill the president, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal on 9 July.

open image in gallery U.S. President Donald Trump spoke to members of the press for the first time aboard the new Air Force One while in flight from RAF Mildenhall AFB to Joint Base Andrews July 8, 2026 after leaving the United Kingdom. Trump, who switched from the old Air Force One to the new Air Force One while in the U.K. is returning from his visit to Ankara, Turkey where he attended the NATO summit ( Getty )

As Trump himself has admitted, he was secretly transported away from Turkey via a ruse involving Air Force One, a catering truck and a second military decoy plane as part of an elaborate “deception operation” after an Iranian assassination threat came to light.

Journalists and several White House personnel had believed they would be traveling with Trump on his return journey to Washington but he was instead smuggled out of the presidential plane and put on board another aircraft .

“I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump said on Tuesday. “They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane. I just have to do what they say.”

“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House Communication Director Steven Cheung said in a statement.

Toilet waste escorted back to US

During the Turkey visit he also went to extreme lengths to protect himself abroad, including reportedly having his human waste carried back from Turkey to prevent any intelligence-gathering about his health, according to The Guardian.

Taking 1,400 staff members with him, including those responsible for transporting the waste, the procedure is reportedly a standard part of the security surrounding the president. Other world leaders including Russian leader Vladimir Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong-Un take similar precautions.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump's route home from July's Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey, via RAF Mildenhall, England ( The Independent )

Social media threats to wife Melania and son Barron

Trump’s wife Melania and son Barron have also been targeted in Iranian propaganda videos including one in July titled “Where to kill Melania” featuring the First Lady in the crosshairs of a gun, as well as an ominous threat ordering their 20-year-old son to “wait for us”.

It appeared to show locations Melania frequently visits and instructions on how to assassinate her. She later opted to skip the White House Correspondents Dinner.

The clip, shared by Tasnim news agency, which is associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was being investigated by the US Secret Service.

It was not the first time they faced calls for their death – a billboard depicting portraits of Trump, Melania and several of the president’s children above coffins draped in American flags was spotted in Tehran’s Palestine Square in July.

Response to assassinations ordered by Trump

Trump ordered the assassination of Iranian general Qasem Soleimani in 2020, sparking condemnation and concern including from Iraqi politicians, the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres as well as US academic Noam Chomsky who called it “an extraordinarily dangerous act”. Soleimani was subsequently revered for his martyrdom across Iran after the killing.

In February 2026, Trump joined forces with Israel to assassinate supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in his compound sparking the ongoing war with Iran.

He has since openly boasted about the deaths of officials in the Iranian government. One of its highest ranking officials, Ali Larijani, had tweeted ominous social media posts threatening the US leader to which Trump had responded: “I couldn’t care less”, before Larijani was killed by the Israeli military.

A woman in Northern Virginia was left looking down the barrel of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer’s gun after she shouted profanities at the federal agents while they were conducting immigration enforcement.

The woman, Carolina Molina, was driving around a parking lot in Falls Church Monday afternoon when law enforcement officers cornered her vehicle and confronted her – accusing Molina of trying to run them over.

In cellphone footage shared on social media, one ICE agent pointed his firearm directly at Molina, accusing her of following the agents around and trying to run them over.

“You need to stop following us. This is your warning… You almost ran us over,” the agent shouted at her.

Molina disputed the allegations, calling the officer “full of s***.” She later shared dashcam video from her vehicle, which showed her first driving past the federal agent’s car and then attempting to drive in front of it before being stopped.

open image in gallery ICE agents in Virginia confronted a woman who shouted insulting profanities at them with a firearm and accused her of trying to run them over – which she says never happened ( tinyandstrongthings / Instagram )

The Independent has asked the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment.

Molina, a licensed counselor who works with immigration lawyers to conduct psychological evaluations, said she was driving in the area to drop off her business cards at lawyers’ offices when she saw the federal agents.

According to the shared dashcam video, Molina rolled down her window and shouted at them as she passed federal agents, who were stopped at an intersection.

“You’re a hoe, you’re f***ed up,” Molina said.

Molina continued to drive around the parking lot but decided to turn around. She said she chose to do so because she didn’t want the ICE agents following her into the immigration lawyer’s office in the event an immigrant was inside.

Once Molina turned around, she passed federal agents’ vehicle again. This time, as she attempted to make a left turn, the agents pulled their car in front of her – stopping her from continuing her ride. Another law enforcement vehicle pulled up behind Molina, preventing her from leaving.

open image in gallery Federal agents accused the Virginia woman of following them and trying to run them over, though she later posted dashcam footage of the incident and accused DHS of lying about the events that took place Monday ( tinyandstrongthings / Instagram )

That’s when a masked agent got out of the car and approached Molina on the driver’s side door, wielding his firearm. Molina began recording with her cellphone.

The agent shouted at Molina: “Are you following us?” to which she responded: “No, I’m not.”

“You need to stop following us,” the agent continued. “This is your warning.”

He added: “You almost ran us over.”

Molina responded: “I didn’t almost run you over. You’re so full of s***.”

The agent yelled back: “Stop playing. Alright? You’re not funny. I will arrest you; keep it up.”

Molina told officers she was a U.S. citizen and told them she had dashcam footage of the incident. Eventually, the agents returned to their vehicle and allowed Molina to leave.

“I know my laws,” Molina told WUSA9. “I’m an American citizen. I have the right. I have my First Amendment rights. I can say what I want and I don’t feel like I should have a gun pointed to my head because you didn’t like being called a hoe.”

open image in gallery Dashcam footage from Carolina Molina, posted online, shows the moment she drove past federal agents and shouted insults at them while in a parking lot ( tinyandstrongthings / Instagram )

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, shared on social media by Molina, that ICE was conducting “targeted immigration enforcement” against undocumented immigrants with criminal charges of hit and run and well as drug trafficking.

“An anti-ICE agitator began to drive her car in circles around our ICE officers and then attempted to harm officers by weaponizing her vehicle against them in an attempt to help illegal aliens get away.”

“Fearing for their safety, ICE officers conducted a vehicle stop of the driver. Necessary background information of the driver was taken and she could face criminal prosecution as a result of her actions.”

News.title: Manchester United v Leeds LIVE: Tielemans set to start as Carrick’s men take on old rivals in Dublin
News.content:

News.title: Ex-Disney head Bob Iger partners with Josh Kushner to buy Los Angeles Lakers for a staggering $12.5 billion
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Billionaire Mark Walter is reportedly selling the Los Angeles Lakers to former Disney CEO Bob Iger and venture capitalist Josh Kushner for a record-breaking $12.5 billion.

"As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world. We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss," Kushner and Iger told ESPN in a statement Wednesday. "Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."

The pair had been involved in the NBA’s expansion process in Las Vegas before unexpectedly shifting their focus to the Lakers and making an aggressive offer to buy the team, sources told ESPN.

The shocking sale comes just one year after Walter, the CEO and chairman of diversified holding company TWG Global, acquired a controlling stake in the Lakers from the Buss family for an estimated $10 billion valuation, setting a record at the time.

“Owning the Los Angeles Lakers has been one of the great honors of my life – an extraordinary investment, but what I will carry with me is the community, the fans, and a city that treats this team as family,” Walter, who purchased the franchise just last year, said in a statement to ESPN. “I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players, and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter. The Lakers belong to Los Angeles, and I have every confidence the best is still ahead.”

open image in gallery Former Disney CEO Bob Iger (pictured) and venture capitalist Josh Kushner are reportedly buying the Los Angeles Lakers for a record-breaking $12.5 billion ( Getty Images for Vanity Fair )

open image in gallery Kushner, 41, is the founder and CEO of venture capital firm Thrive Capital and the co-founder and vice chairman of Oscar Health. His brother is Jared Kushner ( Getty Images )

Walter, 66, has investments across several professional sports teams. Through TWG Global, he has ownership in the Los Angeles Dodgers, Los Angeles Sparks, Premier League soccer club Chelsea and the Professional Women’s Hockey League. He also owns several auto racing teams through TWG Motorsports, including Cadillac’s Formula 1 team.

The reported deal involves only Walter’s ownership of the Lakers, according to ESPN.

Walter built his fortune in the insurance industry and is also facing federal investigations into alleged tax fraud at other companies he runs.

Kushner, 41, is the founder and CEO of venture capital firm Thrive Capital and the co-founder and vice chairman of Oscar Health. In April, Thrive Eternal, a permanent investment vehicle from Thrive Capital, acquired a minority, non-controlling stake in the San Francisco Giants.

open image in gallery The deal would be the highest paid for an American sports franchise ( Getty Images )

He is also the younger brother of Jared Kushner, a former adviser to President Donald Trump who is married to Ivanka Trump. Josh Kushner is married to supermodel Karlie Kloss.

Iger, 75, meanwhile, recently ended his second stint as Disney CEO, handing the role to Josh D’Amaro in March. Iger also has experience in professional sports ownership, as he and his wife, Willow Bay, became controlling owners of the National Women's Soccer League club Angel City FC in July 2024.

Iger and Kushner would take over the Lakers as the franchise enters the post-LeBron James era.

James left in July for the Philadelphia 76ers after eight seasons in LA and one NBA title, leaving Luka Doncic as the team’s new centerpiece. The Lakers have also added big man Walker Kessler and re-signed guard Austin Reaves.

News.title: WHO warns Congo’s Ebola outbreak is on track to become deadliest in history
News.content:
