After 10 years away, York City are back in the EFL!

But it has not been all smooth sailing since. A couple of weeks before the start of the season, manager Stuart Maynard - who led them to promotion with more than 100 points - departed the club.

His replacement Scott Lindsey has not proven popular so far. In his first game in charge York exited the Carabao Cup at the preliminary phase, with fans booing and calling for the return of Maynard.

Not quite the return the Minstermen would have wanted to League Two.

The side they edged to automatic promotion in the National League, Rochdale, have also lost their manager after fighting their way through the play-offs.

McNulty moved on to Stockport, and they have dipped into non-League to appoint their new manager, with Ian Watson joining from National League North side South Shields.

Will Salford City finally get over the line?

Image: Macaulay Langstaff is one of the summer arrivals at Salford City

It is seven years now since Salford City were promoted to League Two, and still they have not managed to get over the line.

Last season was the closest they have come, losing in the play-off final to Notts County. Manager Karl Robinson has since departed, with Peter Cklamovski taking his place, having most recently been in charge of the Malaysia national side.

They have gone big in the transfer market, too. Macaulay Langstaff and Luke Molyneux have already arrived. Could this be the year the club owned by Gary Neville and David Beckham finally reach League One?

Managerial changes in League Two

Elsewhere, there are a lot of new managers to keep an eye on. Chris Hogg has come in at Northampton Town, while another relegated club in Rotherham United have appointed Alex Bruce.

Darrell Clarke takes charge at Tranmere Rovers, Lee Grant is at Walsall and Hayden Mullins will lead Newport County this season.

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 6: Chelsea
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 3rd (NB: this is not necessarily Billy Munday’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 10th

Prospects

After a season of struggle and regression, with two head coaches and two spells under a caretaker, there is cautious optimism that this campaign will bring something like stability. Much of that optimism centres around the appointment of Xabi Alonso, an elite manager with something to prove. There is also an expectation that the young players brought in as part of BlueCo’s £1.8bn splurge in recent years are beginning to come into their best years. There is no European football to complicate the schedule and a return to the Champions League by finishing in the top four or five would suffice for now. More importance will be placed on the domestic cups after a season without trophies.

Alonso’s squad is more rounded than what Enzo Maresca or Liam Rosenior had at their disposal. Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers bring quality to positions where Chelsea were lacking it – at centre-back and out wide. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson – the “uncs” as Tosin Adarabioyo has called them – will contribute as much off the pitch as on it. The signing of Marco Palestra, a specialist wing-back, suggests Alonso wants to be tactically flexible. He has used a back four and a back three in pre-season.

What about Cole Palmer? For so much of his time at Stamford Bridge, Chelsea’s form has been tied to his. When he has struggled to be 100% fit, the team have suffered too. After being omitted from England’s World Cup squad, Palmer had a seven-week break and sought advice from a specialist on the groin injury that hampered him last season. “I got bored after six weeks,” Palmer said after returning for pre-season. “I was sat in Marbella thinking: ‘I want to go back in.’” With the prospect of linking up with Rogers and João Pedro, who has also had a good rest, Palmer has plenty of reasons to be excited.

Off-field picture

July ended with Chelsea being fined £10m and receiving a suspended transfer ban over multiple violations of transfer rules under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. An appeal from the club saved them from a six-point deduction. Chelsea were deemed compliant with the Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules for the three-year period ending in 2025 despite posting an English record £262.4m pre-tax loss for the 2024-25 season. They have not been cowed by failure to qualify for Europe and have spent over £300m on new signings. For the fourth year in a row, Chelsea look likely to start the season without a front-of-shirt sponsor.

Owner-fan relationship

Supporter protests against the ownership of Todd Boehly’s BlueCo have been a frequent sight on matchdays, including before May’s FA Cup final defeat by Manchester City. There have been reservations about the club’s youth-oriented transfer policy from the start and last season’s failings prompted the co-owner Behdad Eghbali to admit the need “to add more ready-made players” to the squad. Whether fans were expecting the arrivals of Welbeck and Henderson is another question. The introduction of a ticket ballot system for home games has also been unpopular with regular match-going supporters.

The manager

It was a bit of a coup for Chelsea to secure Alonso’s services this summer, especially given the Liverpool job was available. The Spaniard has a reputation to rebuild after his dream job at Real Madrid ended in the sack after six months. “I got a scar, now it is healed,” he said. Alonso’s record of developing young players, such as Florian Wirtz, at Bayer Leverkusen while simultaneously delivering silverware is a match made in heaven for the Chelsea hierarchy. One detail to note: Alonso has been appointed as manager, rather than head coach like his predecessors. He has also brought in Austin MacPhee, Aston Villa’s set-piece guru.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Chelsea broke the British transfer record to pry Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Chelsea went one better than Manchester City’s £116m signing of Elliot Anderson by bringing in Rogers, who had been linked with Arsenal, for a new British record fee of £117m. Although he started England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina on the right wing, Rogers has thrived for Aston Villa playing largely off the left and should slot in there nicely at Chelsea. The 24-year-old has proved himself in the Premier League and his best-buddy relationship with his former Manchester City youth teammate Palmer is a major plus. “I can see them linking really well,” Alonso said.

Stat attack

Has anyone checked Chelsea haven’t built a squad of Benjamin Buttons? The average age of their starting XI has decreased over the past three seasons when they were already the youngest team in Premier League history. You can see why they signed Henderson and Welbeck.

Set for a breakthrough

Robert Sánchez is still Chelsea’s No 1 but he may face serious competition this season from the 21-year-old Mike Penders. The goalkeeper, who was third-choice for Belgium at the World Cup, was signed from Genk in 2024 and spent last season on loan at Strasbourg in Ligue 1. The comparisons with Thibaut Courtois, who Chelsea signed from Genk at a similar age, are obvious. Like Courtois, Penders is 6ft 7in and therefore has a massive reach, but he also earns plaudits for his passing. Chances will come in cup competitions, but the clamour for Penders to be first choice might become hard to ignore.

World Cup impact

Enzo Fernández had a rollercoaster of a World Cup. Chelsea’s vice-captain popped up with crucial late goals for Argentina in the knockout stages, including a winning header against Egypt and the equaliser against England. But the abiding memory was his part in Argentina’s unsavoury approach in the final against Spain, where he received one yellow card for dissent and another for sending Pau Cubarsí flying. Real Madrid said in July they had “no intention” of pursuing a move that Fernández seemed to covet earlier this year when he said he would “love” to live in Madrid – comments that earned him a two-game ban under Rosenior. How about living in Manchester? City have been linked.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his father
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi said on Wednesday that he is having doubts about continuing his career following the death of his father last week. Messi’s father, ⁠Jorge, died last week aged 68 at a medical clinic in the Argentinian city of Rosario after a long illness.

In a tribute on Instagram, Messi wrote: “I don’t know what I’m going to ⁠do without you. I ⁠don’t know how ​to move forward. I only played football and now I have quite a few doubts about whether I’m going to keep doing it for much ⁠longer.

“You were by my side from the beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn’t you hold on just ⁠a little longer so we could finish it together?”

Jorge closely accompanied his son throughout his career, beginning ​with his early years at Barcelona. He acted ‌as a crucial pillar of ‌support and, for several years, served as his representative.

The 39-year-old Argentina captain revealed one of the reasons he ‌played in the World Cup, where they finished runners-up to Spain after an extra-time defeat in the final, was because it was his father’s wish.

“You always asked me to play in the last World Cup and a few days before it started was when you got worse,” Messi said. “It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament … Every time a match ended, I would ‌wait and hope for your message. That’s when I realised how real the situation was.”

During the World Cup, Messi experienced mixed emotions after scoring a hat-trick in ​the opening match against Algeria, breaking down in tears while celebrating his first goal. He later explained that his tears were due to “something unrelated to football” after going through “a few difficult, complicated days”.

Messi said he wanted to win the final for his father but he had no energy left to bring home a second World Cup title. “My ⁠legs couldn’t go on any more. This time I tried to push myself beyond my ​physical limits, but I couldn’t. ​I never felt well … We weren’t champions, ​but you don’t know how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were ​right: I had to ‌be there and play ​it.”

Despite his ​grief, the Inter Miami forward pledged to honour his father’s memory through parenting his own children. “I’m going to miss you so much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I will teach them and raise them the way you raised me.”

Sports.title: ‘It’s a nice hobby’: Manchester United’s Janina Leitzig on goalkeeping and gardening
Sports.content:
With some parts of England gearing up for a fifth heatwave of 2026 the new Manchester United goalkeeper Janina Leitzig, a keen gardener, is sympathetic to the precarious health of this reporter’s tomato plants. “You’re not used to so little rain, are you?” she observes. For the time being, after her summer move to Manchester, the former Germany youth international does not have a garden of her own but she reveals that, during her three-and-a-half-year spell at her former club Leicester, homegrown vegetables were her pride and joy.

“I love to do some gardening. Back home, everyone has their own vegetables and it’s just better, it tastes better,” she tells the Guardian. “Being away from home and away from family, of course you have your football friends, but still it can be quite lonely sometimes if you come home from training, so it was really nice to have a garden and to spend time outside. It’s not too much effort, it’s just a nice hobby.”

The 27-year-old got her outdoor fix with a spot of surfing in Cornwall this summer during the off-season, but now the serious business of pre-season is well under way. Her new club Manchester United are heading to La Manga for a training camp between 14 and 19 August, where the focus will have to be less on runner beans and more on running drills.

Leitzig, the former Bayern Munich and Hoffenheim keeper, was sitting down for an interview before it was known that the Spanish coach Eva Olid was to become United’s new manager, but explained why swapping Leicester for United was appealing to her. “It’s such a big club and it’s such a big honour to be here,” Leitzig says.

“I think, for every player, it’s really interesting if you have an offer from Manchester United. First of all, the team is so nice. The characters in here – you can tell it’s a really good and strong team. The training quality is really high. The building and the facilities [at Carrington] are really good; it’s really professional here. [When] the conversations were going on [with United], they just gave me a really good feeling.”

View image in fullscreen Janina Leitzig during a training session at Carrington. Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty Images

Leitzig has signed a contract with United until 2029, after the disappointment of relegation with Leicester last season, but says she has nothing but fond feelings about her former club, who she initially joined on loan in January 2023 before signing permanently that summer.

Looking back at what she learned in the East Midlands, she says: “It was such a special time for me. It was supposed to be only half a year and then it ended up being three-and-a-half. I think that says a lot about how much I liked it there. The people are great and the club is great.

“Obviously we had some tough times and unfortunately the relegation last season was really, really tough and it really hurt, because the club deserves to be in a better position, but I really hope that the girls will do well and I see them soon back in the WSL. It would be great if they could come back up quickly.”

During her time in England, Leitzig has observed an evolution in goalkeeping styles, and she is in a thoughtful mood when discussing what the future might look like for keepers, tactically. On the modern trend of keepers playing out from the back, she says: “To be fair, there was one phase where everyone wanted goalkeepers to play with the feet and I think it’s still really important, but I think there was a phase where it was too much. I think it was a bit overexaggerated at times, so I think it’s coming back now to be more about the basic stuff.

“Obviously you have to switch play and you have to be good with your feet under pressure, but I think the game is going to be more [about] trying to get the ball as quick as possible in the opposite half to then keep the pressure up there and not to try to take such a high risk. It’s going to be interesting.

“I think, because I’m German and Manuel Neuer [her idol] is German, I learned quite early to play with both feet and I was an outfield player initially, so I’m feeling confident about playing with the ball. But saving shots is the best part of goalkeeping.”

The USA keeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce played in 21 of United’s 22 matches in the Women’s Super League last season and Leitzig says they will enjoy working together and helping each other. “They [United] said it’s like a competition [to start in goal]. Obviously it’s really important to have strong goalkeepers, because you never know what happens in the season.

“I will just give my best, I’ll try to bring quality, and then it’s the manager’s decision to decide who’s going to play. But it’s really important that we are a good goalkeeper team, that we support each other and push each other because then everyone can get better.”

United, who finished fourth last season, will get the new WSL season under way on the opening night, at London City Lionesses on 4 September. Leizig concludes by looking ahead to that showdown and says, with fire in her eyes: “To have the first game of the season Friday evening, 7pm, floodlights, it’s just something you’re really excited for. Working in the pre-season you think: ‘When can the [games] finally start,’ so I’m really excited for that game.”

Sports.title: Barcelona make improved £51m bid for Rodri as Manchester City target Fernández
Sports.content:
Barcelona have made an improved bid to Manchester City of around €60m (£51m) for Rodri. This follows Barça’s initial offer of €45m that was rejected out of hand by City.

The Spanish club’s new offer – which may include add-ons – is close to City’s valuation for the 30-year-old who captained Spain to the World Cup and won the Ballon d’Or in 2024.

As the midfielder has declared a preference for Barcelona it seems it is inevitable he will leave. In preparation City are targeting Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández as a potential signing though the west London club’s valuation of around £120m may be too high.

Chelsea are understood to be intent on that price for the attacking midfielder so any transfer may include add-ons. Enzo Maresca is keen on Fernández after working with him for a season-and-a-half at Chelsea before his tenure ended in January.

The 25-year-old was a key member of Maresca’s team that finished fourth and won the Europa Conference in 2024-25 and the Fifa Club World Cup last summer.

If City were to sign Fernández, a World Cup winner with Argentina in 2022, another midfielder could be offloaded, with Tijjani Reijnders a possible candidate to depart.

As Rodri is intent on a move to Barcelona the arrival of Fernández, Chelsea’s captain, would add seniority and leadership to Maresca’s squad and a player whose combative style would offer an edge to City’s play.

City have so far recruited Elliott Anderson for £116m from Nottingham Forest and are close to the signing of Ayyoub Bouaddi for around £85m from Lille.

Chelsea are thought to have enquired about Bournemouth’s Alex Scott as a replacement for Fernández should he leave.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Newcastle’s ‘rock star’ plays the hits but will he find it hard to stay in Toon?
Sports.content:
IN A BLACK AND WHITE TOWN

As rallying cries for the dawn of a golden era go, “I am quite optimistic” is not “ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country”. It did not fit the “I think I am a special one” template set 22 years ago by Netflix’s latest documentary subject. Nor did Matthias Jaissle’s unveiling as Newcastle manager meet the pre-match billing of “fire” and “a rock star” that the club’s chief suit had promised the journalists in attendance. Though, considering the summer of tumult on Tyneside, it was a sensible path to take. Expectations among the Toon Army have certainly lowered since Geordies sunk Tin and donned tea-towel headdresses in celebration of Mike Ashley’s departure and the arrival of a consortium underpinned by the petrodollars of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. As it turned out, Lionel Messi neither ended up mowing the pitch nor selling the pies.

Depending on your perspective, that Newcastle have not yet been crowned Premier League and Bigger Cup champions is down to the servile football authorities bowing down to the hated red cartel or that day of wild celebration being one of false hope. The truth lies probably somewhere in between. A number of missteps pockmarked the last season of Eddie Howe’s reign. The “here we go” arrivals were nowhere near up to snuff. It should, though, be readily accepted that Newcastle enjoyed a good run under Howe, including an actual trophy and two rides on the Bigger Cup fun bus.

The Saudi connection has not paved St James’ Park with black gold (or Texas tea as the Beverly Hillbillies once had it). A pitfall of becoming the plaything of a top-level geopolitical operator is that those geopolitics may get in the way. Gulf states have a few things on their plates at the moment, and the interests of that investment fund stretch beyond a football club 3,000 miles from Riyadh. A new phase is entered; Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães are gone. Some might say the Saudis have lost interest, though Jaissle’s arrival from Al-Ahli, another club in the Pif portfolio, suggests hands are still on the tiller.

As for the new manager, the verdict was that he spoke very well at his premiere. “We were looking at each other with smiles and goosebumps,” he cooed, in describing his and his assistants’ first look at the stadium. Realism was offered in admitting a “vacuum” now those assets have been flogged off but there was no preview of the touchline histrionics various profiles have promised. Jaissle also followed the recent but now ingrained tradition of shaking each of his future interrogators’ hands. A classy gesture? A power move? Take your pick. Howe’s departure, and the loss of those big names, has returned Newcastle to the state of flux that was long their usual state of existence. How long can Jaissle’s calm and collected deportment last? How long can measured optimism sustain?

Sports.title: Championship angst: why the sense of rejuvenation in EFL is not universal
Sports.content:
A new season is supposed to be about renewed hope and optimism, a fresh campaign opening up a world of possibilities, a clean slate. But with the English Football League due to kick off on Friday night when Wolves host Blackburn in the Championship, the sense of rejuvenation is not universal.

The lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome. Wolves and West Ham, hitherto established Premier League clubs, have dropped into the second tier. Others such as Burnley, Middlesbrough and Southampton anticipate a promotion push. So perhaps supporters of those who are not enjoying parachute payment riches and squads still packed with top-flight talent are wise to feel cautious. Some fear a long slog of a season to come.

Blackburn fans, for example, saw their side scrape to the safety of a 20th-place finish last season, therefore would be forgiven for tempering their expectations before the trip to Molineux. Tony Mowbray has been brought back to Ewood Park as an experienced guiding hand, but the 62-year-old has a huge task to avoid a relegation battle.

Fans believe the Rovers owners and the club’s head of football operations, Rudy Gestede, have sold Mowbray short on players heading into the season, particularly in midfield. The 34-year-old Sam Morsy – described by Mowbray as “a real man, a soldier” – has added steel to that area of the pitch with his free transfer, but after Moussa Baradji and Jayden Fevrier he is only the third addition at Blackburn this summer. Mowbray wants and needs more.

“I’m a bit greedy for good players,” he said. “I keep saying to Rudy: ‘I just want good players, doesn’t really matter where they come from, what age they are.’ I want to see personality on the pitch, players who are desperate to win.”

Blackburn edged past Burton 2-1 in the Carabao Cup first round last week, though they required late goals from Andri Gudjohnsen and Fevrier, who Mowbray believes can bring “magic” on the right wing after signing from Stockport.

View image in fullscreen Bolton Wanderers celebrated victory in the League One playoff final but a tricky season lies ahead. Photograph: Nigel French/PA

Down the road, there are two other Championship clubs feeling a similar sense of trepidation before the new campaign, and they meet at the Toughsheet Stadium on Saturday lunchtime, a game that could set the tone for their seasons. Bolton should still be on cloud nine; they finished last season with a 4-1 demolition of Stockport in the League One playoff final. Yet as the football world has witnessed this summer at York – where the manager, Stuart Maynard, was sacked and replaced by Scott Lindsey, despite winning the National League with 108 points – the afterglow of promotion can be short-lived. Reality bites quick.

And such is the chasm between the second and third tiers nowadays, the need for Steven Schumacher’s side to strengthen fast became paramount after that glorious day at Wembley. David Watson, Ben Davies, Akin Famewo, Luca Stephenson, Kyliane Dong and Gaizka Larrazabal have all arrived, but there is a feeling among the fanbase that a marquee addition is needed, especially in attack where they risk asking too much of the striker Sam Dalby. Schumacher’s admission last week that Bolton “can’t afford to waste money” rang alarm bells with the fanbase. There is not an embarrassment of riches in the pot but forward players must be signed.

“We know we’re short, especially at the top end of the pitch,” Schumacher said. “Our budget isn’t massive so we need to make sure we get the right players in, rather than just signing anybody to fill numbers. We need to try and consolidate this year, rebuild, get some more finances behind us, bring in a better squad that can keep us at this level, and then kick on.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Schumacher said that “this part of the journey is an exciting one” but it seems negativity among some fans has kicked in before a Championship ball has been kicked. A 1-0 defeat against Sheffield Wednesday in the Carabao Cup reinforced concerns around goalscoring, or the lack of it. Max Dean of Gent is coveted, but the striker is just 22 and his English football experience is limited to a short spell at MK Dons.

Preston will hope to take advantage of the uncertainty around Bolton on Saturday, but Paul Heckingbottom has endured his own problems in the transfer market this summer. A public spat with Ben Whiteman over the midfielder’s desire to join Wrexham left a cloud hanging above the club and saw the Lilywhites lose their club captain. Heckingbottom said Whiteman “crossed a line” and was frustrated by the saga.

Money has been spent at Deepdale this summer with Alfie Devine brought in from Tottenham for a fee in the region of £6m, while Callum Lang “feels like a new signing” according to Heckingbottom, having arrived in January for around £2m before getting injured. So the pressure is on Heckingbottom perhaps like never before. A run of just four wins from their final 20 matches of last season prompted a few fan murmurs of discontent towards the manager. With Preston almost investing £1.5m to install a modern hybrid pitch at Deepdale, the club expect better than last season’s 14th-place finish, but expectations can weigh heavy.

Sports.title: ‘It is just smelling football’: Tielemans says adjusting to life at United has come naturally
Sports.content:
Youri Tielemans has stated that adjusting to Michael Carrick’s vision for Manchester United has been as easy as “smelling football” for the vastly experienced £35m midfield signing.

The 29-year-old, who joined from Aston Villa last month, made his debut for Anderlecht at the age of 16. He has been integrating with the United squad during the past 10 days of the club’s pre-season tour, making his first appearance in the 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg on Saturday.

Tielemans left Belgium for Monaco in 2017 and joined Leicester in 2019, before signing for Villa four years later and has 579 career appearances, so any demands from Carrick do not faze him.

Tielemans said: “He has got his structure. He wants to have the ball, he wants to press in certain ways, you know. It might be different than what you are used to, what I have been used to before, but it is logical things in my opinion. It is just smelling football, and that is what I have been doing from when I was young at Anderlecht.

“So for me, nothing changes, but it just needs to gel together. Then when you follow those principles, then you can add your offensive qualities, especially in the last third where everything is a bit more in freedom, without obviously overcommitting and keeping the defensive line in place, then I think we can do good things.”

Tielemans was limited to only 25 starts in the Premier League last season because of injury and also sustained a hamstring problem in the warm-up before Belgium’s World Cup quarter-final against Spain in July. Yet despite this and having already played for 13 years in midfield, Tielemans denied that Carrick will need to rest him on occasion.

He said: “Not really. The thing is, at the World Cup, I think we played 120 minutes against Senegal [before Spain], and from there we had less time in between games. So we played the US I think three or four days later [actually five days] and then three days later we played against Spain. In the warm-up, my body just switched off for some reason. Now, I do not think I am a player that I absolutely need a rest. Obviously, there are a lot of games and the manager needs to manage the team, but when I am good I am good, you know.

“Unfortunately, my body is … when it does not go well, then I will know straight away and I will alert the manager, but it does not happen often.”

United previously showed interest in signing the Belgium captain, reportedly in 2019 and 2022. “There has been two times that I spoke with the club, but it did not achieve to anything, so I was just very calm about it. It was way after Anderlecht,” Tielemans said.

United, who triggered his release clause, did not face any competition to sign the player. “Not that I am aware of, no,” Tielemans said.

Sports.title: Saudi Pro League tries to move on from era of ageing megastar but big names still loom | John Duerden
Sports.content:
There is no Mohamed Salah in the new Saudi Pro League season that kicks off on Thursday and while the era of the ageing megastar is ending, there is still the strong chance the next few months will be dominated by Cristiano Ronaldo. The 41-year-old is 24 shy of 1,000 career goals and, with the five-time Ballon d’Or winner having scored 102 in 107 league games for Al-Nassr, the milestone could – should – be reached this season.

Huge as that will be, just how it fits into the plans of the league is unclear. This is the fourth season since the spending started with $957m splashed out in the summer of 2023. It produced thousands of articles, dozens of international broadcasting deals and untold numbers of people worldwide sporting the yellow CR7 Al-Nassr shirt. Now, though, the focus is on getting a little more value for money and lifting not just the clubs, but the standard of Saudi Arabian football in general.

An early World Cup elimination provoked plenty of questions (even if later results showed that draws against Uruguay and an impressive Cape Verde plus a sole defeat against Spain, the eventual champions, was not quite as bad as it first looked), with the main one being whether the money spent on the local league had resulted in a better standard of local players. As yet, it does not seem to be the case.

The league does not yet supply talent to Europe or anywhere else. Of the 26-man World Cup squad only the right-back, Saud Abdulhamid, of Lens, plays overseas. The consensus is that this has to change and is heightened by the worry that too many of those who stay home do not play enough. Locals are often squeezed out by foreign talents, especially when it comes to creative, goalscoring and goalkeeping positions.

The big spending has undoubtedly improved the standard of teams in general – Saudi sides have had increased success in Asian club competitions, but the national side has yet to see the benefit.

While many expected Salah to choose the Red Sea over the Black Sea port of Trabzonspor, the determination to sign the Egyptian seemed to have lessened over the past few months (and that is assuming Salah ever considered Saudi Arabia as his first choice).

The biggest name in the Arab footballing world would have been quite a draw, even if the 34-year-old no longer fits the preferred model, which is trying to sign younger players who have a resale value when they return to Europe.

Will that be the case for Crysencio Summerville, the biggest signing of the summer so far, who joined Al-Hilal for around €80m? If all goes well, the 24-year-old Netherlands winger can spend some time in Riyadh and, one day, head back to Europe for another hefty fee.

There have been the usual criticisms of Summerville choosing money over ambition, but ambition is part of the Hilal DNA. With 19 league titles and four Asian championships, coming second again will not be acceptable even if the team were undefeated through the whole campaign.

The Blues, sold by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) in April, still have Karim Benzema, Rúben Neves, Theo Hernández, Yassine Bounou, Kalidou Koulibaly and more, so the pressure is on the head coach, Simone Inzaghi, to retake the title from the yellow half of Riyadh.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Saud Abdulhamid is the only player from Saudi Arabia to play overseas, with Lens. Photograph: Icon Sport/Alamy

Ronaldo lifted that trophy in May for Al‑Nassr, a triumph soon followed by the exit of Jorge Jesus to take over as the Portugal head coach. He has been replaced by Ange Postecoglou. The former Tottenham manager has Sadio Mané, Kingsley Coman and João Félix at his disposal, but the club have financial problems that have meant, as yet, there have not been many incomings. A first Asian Champions League title would go down well.

That crown belongs to Al‑Ahli who, after winning their second successive continental title in April, were ready to focus on domestic matters this season and a second SPL title since 1984. It was all looking good, but just a few days before the start, the head coach, Matthias Jaissle, left for Newcastle. The Greens and the Magpies share the same owner, PIF, but this was a decision that did not go down well in Jeddah. The appointment of Arne Slot’s former assistant Marino Pusic is not seen as especially exciting.

Jaissle’s departure also came as a shock to Jeddah rivals Al-Ittihad, who struggled last season. Just a day or so before Jaissle’s departure, the Tigers followed their rivals in hiring a 38-year-old German, whose career as a defender had also been cut short by injury and had experience at RB Salzburg. Jens Wissing has a big job ahead.

Al-Qadsiah are the last of the contenders. If Brendan Rodgers can improve on the fourth-place finish of last season and also win a first trophy since 1984, that will be enough for the Aramco‑backed club.

There is now a genuine “big five” that provides challenges for the others, but perhaps they can progress by giving more playing time and opportunities to local players that would, in the long run, be better for the league than signing Salah, and others, in their mid-30s.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi says 'I don't know how to go on' and hints he will QUIT football as he breaks his silence on dad Jorge's death aged 68
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo paid tribute to the late father of his great rival, Lionel Messi, with a touching message on social media.

Lionel Messi has hinted he will retire from football following the devastating death of his father, Jorge, who was an integral figure in the career of his legendary son.

Jorge died on August 7 following a battle with illness that overshadowed the Argentina captain's mesmerising World Cup campaign in the United States, in which he led his team to the final.

Lionel, who broke down in tears following Argentina's group stage win over Algeria while Jorge's health was deteriorating, shared a heartbreaking letter to his father on Instagram – in which he casts doubt over his playing future.

'Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. It hasn't sunk in yet, or rather, I don't want to accept it. It's very difficult for me to imagine never seeing you again, never talking to you again. I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you left too soon. We still had so much to enjoy together.

'I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I only played football and now I have serious doubts that I'll continue doing that for much longer. You were by my side from the beginning, it was so close to the end. Why couldn't you hold on that little bit longer and we could have finished together?'

Ronaldo replied to the post, saying: 'A huge hug to you and yours in these tough times, Leo. Much strength.'

The Portuguese legend knows of Messi's heartache only too well after losing his father, Jose Dinis Aveiro, in 2005 to an alcoholism-related live condition when he was aged just 20.

'I really don’t know my father 100 per cent,' Ronaldo told Piers Morgan in 2019. 'He was a drunk person. I never spoke with him, like a normal conversation. It was hard.'

Messi revealed that his father was the driving force behind his decision to play at this summer's World Cup, but his ageing legs prevented him from bringing the trophy home – with Spain winning 1-0 in the New York final.

Lionel Messi has thanked fans for their support following the death of his father Jorge (left)

Messi's father and agent died in Rosario, Argentina on Friday August 7

Jorge's death saw an outpouring of emotional tributes from the football world, including from Messi's first team Newell's Old Boys, as well as Barcelona and Argentina.

'You kept asking me to play in the last World Cup, and just a few days before it started, you got worse. It was the first time you wouldn't be in a tournament, but Mom kept telling me you'd get better and be well enough to travel. I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel.

'Every time a game ended, I waited and missed your message. That's when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn't stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and for you to see a game. We reached the final and you couldn't be there. I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't, my legs couldn't take it anymore. This time I tried to go against my physical limitations, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel well.

'When I arrived, you thought we'd lost the final on penalties. We couldn't talk about anything that happened. You couldn't enjoy any of it. We didn't win the championship, but you don't know how much we enjoyed every game. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play.

'I'm telling you this because it was the only thing we couldn't talk about, because you already know everything else. We used to talk every day and see each other whenever possible, given my commitments.'

Messi missed Inter Miami's defeat by Monterrey on Sunday to return home in the wake of his father's passing, and thanked fans for their well wishes.

He added on his Instagram stories: 'I want to sincerely thank everyone for all the love, respect and enormous consideration you have shown me and my family during this incredibly painful time following the loss of my dad.

'Thank you for being there for us, for every message, every gesture and, above all, for respecting our grief and our privacy.'

Lionel Messi's father Jorge, pictured at the 2022 World Cup final, died at the age of 68

MESSI STATEMENT IN FULL 'Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. It hasn't sunk in yet, or rather, I don't want to accept it. It's very difficult for me to imagine never seeing you again, never talking to you again. I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you left too soon. We still had so much to enjoy together.' You kept asking me to play in the last World Cup, and just a few days before it started, you got worse. It was the first time you wouldn't be in a tournament, but Mom kept telling me you'd get better and be well enough to travel. I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel. Every time a game ended, I waited and missed your message. That's when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn't stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and for you to see a game. We reached the final and you couldn't be there. I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't, my legs couldn't take it anymore. This time I tried to go against my physical limitations, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel well. When I arrived, you thought we'd lost the final on penalties. We couldn't talk about anything that happened. You couldn't enjoy any of it. We didn't win the championship, but you don't know how much we enjoyed every game. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play. I'm telling you this because it was the only thing we couldn't talk about, because you already know everything else. We used to talk every day and see each other whenever possible, given my commitments. I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I only played football and now I have serious doubts that I'll continue doing that for much longer. You were by my side from the beginning, it was so close to the end. Why couldn't you hold on that little bit longer and we could have finished together? I know that his happiness was seeing his family well, his wife, his children and, above all, without others knowing, seeing me play. It's always been like this since I was little. You'd take me to all the practices as soon as you got home from work. Many times, Mom would take me because you were working. Obviously, you never missed a game. How you suffered watching me, and how you enjoyed it, even though you never gave me many compliments. You were a father, a friend, and a businessman. You were always the person you needed to be in every situation and you never made a mistake. Aside from a few demands or arguments, you were always right. In the end, things always turned out exactly as you said. I will miss you very much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I teach and educate them as you did with me. Rest in peace and watch over us from up there as you did here. Thank you for everything. I love you, Dad.

Messi also posted a picture with his father, captioned: 'I love you, pa' in Spanish.

Football legend Messi was extremely close to his father, who also operated as his agent and de facto business manager throughout his career, overseeing his son's multi-million dollar empire off the pitch.

In recent months, though, the patriarch of the family had been dealing with an as-yet-unconfirmed medical issue that had seen him taken to hospital in his home country.

His illness first came to light when Lionel, 39, cried on the pitch at the World Cup in a rare public display of emotion.

After scoring a hat-trick against Algeria in Argentina's opening group game in Kansas City, Messi was questioned by journalists and said: 'No, honestly it's something completely unrelated to sports. It's been a few difficult days, complicated.'

Just hours later, journalist Eduardo Feinmann explained the reason for the tears in an interview on Radio Mitre, one of the country's most listened-to stations.

'This has to do with his father. His father is not in good health,' he said. 'For quite some time now, several months, since last year.

'And this week there were some situations that slightly worsened his health, and Messi is going through this internal struggle. In other words, like any human being.'

It has since been reported that Jorge suffered a 'medical episode' at his home in January of this year, and he was hospitalised as a result.

In the aftermath, he was said to have undergone cardiovascular and neurological tests, but no official diagnosis was shared by the family, who sought to keep Jorge's health out of the media.

Jorge's health became headline news again in June, when a broadcaster in Argentina falsely claimed he had died – before later issuing an emotional apology and stepping down from her job.

Lionel is the third of four children of Jorge and his wife Celia Cuccittini, and the pair remained together until his death.

They married in 1978 and split their time between Rosario and Miami, where their footballing superstar son currently plays for David Beckham's Inter Miami in Major League Soccer (MLS).

Before becoming Lionel's agent, Jorge worked for a steel manufacturer in Villa Constitucion, meeting his wife as a young man in Rosario – where the family then grew up.

Messi stands in front of his family (including father Jorge (third left) in Rosario in October 2003

Jorge arrives at son Lionel's wedding in 2017 with his wife Celia (L) and daughter Maria (R)

Messi has two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matias, and a younger sister, Maria Sol.

Jorge has been at Messi's side throughout his historic career, which began in Argentina with Newell's Old Boys, before he moved to Spain to join Barcelona's famed La Masia academy in 2000.

He became the greatest of all-time in an incredible 21 years in Barcelona, before stunning the world with a move to Paris Saint-Germain – orchestrated by Jorge – in 2021.

After two seasons in the French capital, he moved to MLS and Inter Miami, where he remains to this day at the age of 39.

While Lionel's career has been magical on the pitch, it has not been without controversy off it, with Jorge famously by his son's side throughout his tax fraud case in 2016.

The pair sat together in front of the court, with Jorge in his role as his son's business manager, with the prosecution alleging that Messi failed to properly pay tax on income from his image rights between 2007 and 2009.

Ultimately, both father and son were convicted of three tax offenses, initially each receiving suspended 21-month prison sentences.

Jorge's sentence was subsequently reduced to 15 months upon review in 2017 by Spain's Supreme Court, with the pair also hit with substantial fines.

Sports.title: The winners, losers and likely bolters for England's 2027 World Cup campaign from new EPS squad - and why this team badly needs an injection of fresh blood, writes ALEX BYWATER
Sports.content:
Once the management speak had been waded through, a clear picture emerged from England's 25-man list of enhanced Elite Player Squad (EPS) contracts for the upcoming season of who Steve Borthwick trusts for the 2027 World Cup.

The winners? Alex Coles, Seb Atkinson and Guy Pepper. The losers? Ollie Lawrence, Tom Roebuck and Elliot Daly. Tom Willis is also now absent after the No 8 decided to rule himself out of England contention by signing for Bordeaux.

Borthwick has not made wholesale changes to the core squad, who each receive in the region of £150,000 from the RFU and are managed more closely by the head coach and his staff. And an EPS contract is no guarantee of Test selection. But it does provide a clue as to what Borthwick is thinking.

Coles’ addition is the most noteworthy, after the Northampton lock’s impressive international progression in the past year. He’s been involved in all of England’s past 12 Tests and went well at lock in the summer’s Nations Championship matches while captain Maro Itoje was rested.

Coles’ development, the return to fitness of the hard-hitting George Martin and Ollie Chessum’s new position on the blindside flank means Borthwick is not short of lineout forwards. Like Chessum, Coles can also play in the back-row and such versatility can be invaluable at World Cups.

Itoje certainly has a job on his hands to return to the starting team, even if the most likely lock combination for the autumn will be him alongside Martin in the second row, with Chessum wearing No6.

Alex Coles’ addition is the most noteworthy, after the Northampton lock’s impressive international progression in the past year

Guy Pepper, who now has 15 caps, has been rewarded for his progress with an EPS contract

ENGLAND'S EPS CONTRACTS, 2026-27 Seb Atkinson (Gloucester), Fin Baxter (Harlequins), Ollie Chessum (Leicester Tigers), Alex Coles (Northampton Saints), Luke Cowan-Dickie (Sale Sharks), Tom Curry (Sale Sharks), Ben Earl (Saracens), Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (Exeter Chiefs), George Ford (Sale Sharks), Tommy Freeman (Northampton Saints), George Furbank (Harlequins), Ellis Genge (Bristol Bears), Jamie George (Saracens), Joe Heyes (Leicester Tigers), Maro Itoje (Saracens), George Martin (Saracens), Alex Mitchell (Northampton Saints), Asher Opoku-Fordjour (Sale Sharks), Guy Pepper (Bath), Henry Pollock (Northampton Saints), Henry Slade (Exeter Chiefs), Fin Smith (Northampton Saints), Marcus Smith (Harlequins), Will Stuart (Bath), Jack van Poortvliet (Leicester Tigers).

Coles, however, will certainly not give up his starting shirt without a fight. His ability to do the nasty, unseen work combined with the ball-playing ability he has honed winning two PREM Rugby titles with the Saints gives him a point of difference.

Alongside Coles, Gloucester centre Atkinson, Bath flanker Pepper, Leicester scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet and Sale prop Asher Opoku-Fordjour are all new faces on the EPS list.

Atkinson’s replacing of Lawrence as one of the centre options is also significant and a blow for the latter, though it may just provide the kick up the backside he needs to return to his best.

A year out from the World Cup, one of the biggest problems England have is that their midfield pairing is still as clear as mud. A fully firing Lawrence has to be in the mix.

On the whole, England’s squad is ripe for a bolter or two to come in and shake-up the established order - perhaps Northampton duo George Hendy and Archie McParland, or Harlequins' 20-year-old scrum-half Lucas Friday.

Noah Caluori and Benhard Janse van Rensburg could upset the apple cart and add an injection of fresh blood into the squad

Of the latest 25-man party, 20 were also named this time last year and the team then went on to produce the worst Six Nations in England’s history, losing four of the five matches.

Some have argued EPS contracts breed a degree of comfort in selection which should always be absent at international level. Borthwick clearly feels different. He knows the ones he trusts and has kept the faith. Noah Caluori and Benhard Janse van Rensburg could upset the apple cart.

You get the feeling England would certainly benefit from an injection of fresh blood after a disappointing 2026. That needs to change because right now, it is hard to make a case for Borthwick’s men being genuine World Cup contenders.

Sports.title: Revealed: Why Andoni Iraola always starts slowly at new clubs, the warning signs in Liverpool's pre-season and his gruelling training sessions to prepare players for his style that make them 'sick'
Sports.content:
After three months in charge of Bournemouth, Andoni Iraola’s job security was under intense scrutiny. The Basque boss, relatively unknown to English fans, had lost six and drawn three of his first nine league games. He did not win one until October 28 and was promptly thrashed 6-1 at Manchester City in the following game. Externally, the noise was deafening, especially after he had been installed in place of Gary O'Neil to some surprise in the summer. But sticking by him was Bournemouth's only option and staffers were quick to dismiss reports of a potential sacking. They were right to do so, as Iraola turned his side's fortunes around. After no wins in the first nine, they won seven of the next nine, losing only one. From a sinking ship to cruising. But slow starts are a concerning theme for the new Liverpool manager. In his first job at AEK Larnaca in Cyprus, he was sacked by mid-January. At Spanish second-division club Mirandes, Iraola won one, drew five and lost four in his first ten fixtures. It was somewhat better at Rayo Vallecano, however given the club were expected to challenge for promotion, just five wins in the first 11 was nothing special. With all due respect to Rayo, who were Conference League runners-up last season, and Bournemouth, who will play in this year's Europa League, there are certain things you can get away with at smaller clubs, but which will not fly at Anfield. Slow starts are a concerning theme for new Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola And with all due respect to his former sides such as Rayo Vallecano, there are some things you can get away with at smaller clubs that will not fly at Liverpool

Your browser does not support iframes.

And then consider his comments after the 3-2 defeat by Monaco in a pre-season friendly last Sunday. Iraola said that his side played a good first 30 minutes but ‘they don't have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this’. It came seven days after a 4-2 loss to Leeds in Chicago where the match followed a similar theme: Liverpool start well, go two goals up, look in fine fettle heading into the break, then capitulate and lose. Now, there is a caveat. Aside from it being pre-season and with a good handful of players not being fully fit after the World Cup summer, Liverpool’s first-half XI in the last two friendlies will not be too dissimilar to the one that starts the opening game of the season away at Newcastle on August 23. Take your best players out for the second half, as Iraola has done, and it should be no surprise that it all falls apart. Iraola’s system is incredibly physically demanding and the buzzword of pre-season was intensity, with Dominik Szoboszlai insisting the ‘intensity we have been missing is back’. Players have ‘felt sick’ at the end of training given the gruelling nature of the new regime. One thing fans criticised Arne Slot for was a lack of such intensity, though worries that the squad were given too many days off was a myth. While they had clearly lost an edge and maybe belief or effort, they worked the same number of hours as they did when winning the league. Regardless, things have changed now and players will need a period of becoming hardened to the new, all-action style. Some players have spoken of having ‘no legs left’, but Iraola slaps down a punishment for those who lose training drills: a sprint to the other end of the pitch and back. Bournemouth ranked first in the Premier League last season for direct attacks and third when it came to high turnovers, defined as any possession sequence that starts in open play and begins 40 metres or fewer from the opponent's goal. Simon Brundish, a sports science expert, points out that the problem is players' ability to sprint repeatedly, and be as explosive on sprint No 10 as they were on sprint No 1. He insists this is what vanishes fastest at the end of the season, and can take between four to eight weeks to properly rebuild. Iraola’s system is incredibly physically demanding and the buzzword of pre-season was intensity, with Dominik Szoboszlai insisting the ‘intensity we have been missing is back’ Worryingly, Iraola admitted after the 3-2 home defeat by Monaco last weekend that his players can only handle his style for around 30 minutes

Your browser does not support iframes.

‘Iraola’s actual system is brutal on a specific quality: running just under a full sprint, done together, repeatedly, as a unit,’ says Brundish. ‘Bournemouth did 4.1km of that per game, Liverpool did 1.4km (last season's averages). Total sprint numbers were basically the same between the two teams. It’s not speed they're short on. It’s making it repeatable.’ Aside from the gruelling nature of the style, players will also need time to adapt tactically to the differences between Slot and Iraola. When speaking to Daily Mail Sport last year, Bournemouth forward Justin Kluivert explained: ‘It took everyone a while to understand. He had a rough start with a lot of losses but the club believed in him, we believed in him – and that is paying off now. He has improved my game significantly… he played me in a different role so I thank Andoni for that… he had a good vision!’ Another former Cherry, Antoine Semenyo, said on the In The Mixer podcast: ‘I didn't see it at the start. When he came in, he had his way of playing and it was very new to us, the way he structured the weeks. ‘We didn't really have any days off, so it's very hard for a team to go from having Wednesday and Sunday off to having no days off. It was very different at the start. The results weren't going our way and the fans were saying he needs to be sacked. Everyone slowly got used to the system and it just went up from there.’ Iraola, for the record, has shot down Semenyo’s suggestion that the group have no time off – though this pre-season at Liverpool has been particularly demanding. After landing back from the US tour on Monday, the Reds were given Tuesday off and then back on Wednesday. Iraola is not making any early excuses, but it is worth keeping an eye on whether Liverpool come out of the blocks flying, as they have done in previous seasons. In Jurgen Klopp's final campaign, the Reds won five and drew one of their first six league games. The following year, Slot secured 11 wins in the first 13 games, and it took until the start of April for him to lose for the second time. Last term, they won the first five games and looked primed to retain their Premier League title, but then won only 12 of the remaining 33. Liverpool players face a difficult task in adapting to the repeated sprints that Iraola demanded from his Bournemouth side ‘It took everyone a while to understand,' Bournemouth's Justin Kluivert told us. 'He had a rough start with a lot of losses but they believed in him, we believed in him – and it is paying off' Iraola knows this league is a marathon not a sprint, but is also realistic that he must pick up some wins early in the campaign when his team are not at full capacity, physically or tactically. There is a funny quirk that every manager Iraola will face until mid-October is also new to their job. His first six league fixtures are against Matthias Jaissle, Oliver Glasner, O’Neil, Alvaro Arbeloa, his Bournemouth successor Marco Rose and Enzo Maresca. So Liverpool may look slightly off the pace now but they are certainly not the only ones, and will hope to be boosted by sharp starts from Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz in their sophomore seasons. As Iraola said this week: ‘I would like to say on the first day, we are going to be perfect, everyone will be in place, but probably it is not going to be like this. We will have to do this as quickly as possible.’

Sports.title: 'We're the club everybody hates this year, and I don't really care': Inside the dark cloud of Southampton's post-Spygate summer - how Tonda Eckert is already preparing for potential ban, when club expect verdict and why this season is 'now or never'
Sports.content:
'We're the club everybody hates this year, and I don't really care': Inside the dark cloud of Southampton's post-Spygate summer - how Tonda Eckert is already preparing for potential ban, when club expect verdict and why this season is 'now or never'

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Tonda Eckert enjoys a book metaphor. That much became apparent last Thursday, when this most unsaintly of managers was presented to around 100 Southampton fans at St Mary’s Stadium.

It was a supporters’ forum, so there was the usual array of questions on season tickets and the like, but a single topic dominated the hour-long session.

And there was no surprise in that, because you cannot talk about Southampton’s forthcoming season in the Championship without discussing how the previous campaign ended – Spygate won’t be forgotten in a hurry.

For Eckert, the 33-year-old German at the heart of a scandal, the espionage drama that saw his side expelled in disgrace from the play-offs three months ago and deducted four points from the upcoming campaign is one he cannot outrun; it cannot be disguised by an Eastleigh tracksuit or parked behind an intern in the trees.

Indeed, his job might still be lost in the coming weeks amid the ongoing aftershocks of a remarkable story broken by Craig Hope in the Daily Mail last May.

But last week, in front of those supporters, Eckert sought refuge in the promises of a brighter future. That’s where the metaphors came into it.

There is a cloud still hanging over the future of Southampton boss Tonda Eckert

You cannot talk about Southampton’s forthcoming season in the Championship without discussing how the previous campaign ended – with intern William Salt caught spying

‘I understand that it feels like there's a page that's been ripped out of the book,’ he said. ‘I do believe there are many chapters of memories and as much as we want them all to be positive, I think that it's one of the toughest that the football club has had.

‘But it's not written to the last page yet. For me, there's much more to come. I just hope I will be sitting here in 12 months and talking about the Premier League.’

It is not known if Eckert is a Bond fan. Likewise, we can only speculate facetiously if memoirs might one day emerge from players who were robbed of their shot at the top flight. Working title: The Spy Who Screwed Me.

For the time being, Southampton are a club desperate to move on, starting with their Championship opener at Watford on Sunday. Even factoring in the burden of starting on minus four points, Eckert’s squad is sufficiently strong for a run at promotion. They are ranked fifth or sixth with most bookmakers to go up.

But they are also trapped in limbo, because Eckert remains the subject of a serious FA misconduct charge over his role in the deployment of analysts to spy on Middlesbrough, Ipswich and Oxford United last season. Having already admitted his complicity in the Middlesbrough and Oxford capers to the EFL enquiries, he exists on perilous terrain.

Daily Mail Sport understands a verdict is highly unlikely to be issued prior to the weekend and sources at Southampton believe it could be as far off as September.

But the key point would be the length of any sanction and whether the club’s owner, Serbian billionaire media mogul Dragan Solak, can maintain his robust backing of Eckert in the event he is hit with a huge suspension.

In June, Solak accepted his loyalty to a talented, tainted manager does have limits, and told the Southern Daily Echo: ‘If they ban him, we will appeal. If we lose the appeal, and it's such a long ban, we'll have to take a new manager. We can't leave the club unmanaged.’

Southampton were booted out of the play-offs, hit with a four-point deduction this season and became the laughing stock of English football when the Daily Mail broke the Spygate story

The key point for Eckert would be the length of any sanction and whether the club’s owner Dragan Solak (pictured) maintains his robust backing if the boss is hit with a lengthy ban

Led by the likes of midfielder Finn Azaz (right), Southampton are confident they can reach the Premier League this season

For Eckert, there is little comfort to be found in the precedents for this kind of scenario – FIFA handed a one-year ban to the former coach of Canada women, Bev Priestman, after a drone was flown over a New Zealand training session at the 2024 Olympics.

We might add here that Eckert did apologise earlier in the summer, albeit belatedly. There is also some merit to be found in Southampton’s view that they have been severely punished already by the EFL.

But the flipside to any leniency was graphically spelled out within the EFL’s written reasonings – piecing together the accounts of witnesses, they painted a deplorable picture of the pressures placed on Eckert’s analysts to perform nefarious tasks.

Eckert, for his part, has alluded to hitherto undisclosed contexts, which presumably go beyond the thin excuse that spying is common on the continent. On Thursday, he spoke of ‘an image created that I think is very far away from the truth’, but only time will tell if his version of reality offers a convincing mitigation to the FA.

Either way, Eckert has been preparing for a period away from the technical area. When Southampton played Preussen-Munster in a friendly earlier this month, Eckert watched from the stands and trialled the feasibility of transmitting his instructions to the bench. As a solution, it might suffice for a handful of games, but surely not the bulk of a 46-match league season with the riches of the Premier League at stake.

Ostensibly, there is less concern around the health of Eckert’s squad, to which Manchester City striker Divin Mubama was added on loan on Tuesday. Despite the loss of last season’s joint-top scorer Ross Stewart to Swansea and the £30million sale of influential midfielder Shea Charles to Fulham, Southampton have the nucleus of the group that finished fourth last season with a 21-game unbeaten run, including the two play-off ties against Middlesbrough. They also knocked Arsenal out of the FA Cup.

An unknown at this stage is whether any internal resentment will hang over from how the campaign ended, because in those initial days, post-expulsion, the dressing room anger was real.

We have previously reported that there was a consideration of legal action from some players towards their club over lost bonuses, but Daily Mail Sport understands that never materialised into action.

All public noises from the squad claim there is no ill-feeling towards the manager. Captain Jack Stephens said this month they are ‘fully behind’ Eckert

Eckert has even been preparing for a period away from the technical area, using friendlies to sit in the stands and trial the feasibility of transmitting his instructions to the bench

Contrary to a rumour among some agents, multiple figures around the first team also insisted to us that there was never a sweetener offered by the club to settle the bonuses that would have been paid for promotion. Some players would have been due as much as £250,000 had they reached the Premier League.

It is unclear whether any enhanced compensation will be worked into this season’s bonus structure – Daily Mail Sport has been told elements of those conversations with the club have been deferred until next month – but all public noises from the squad claim there is no ill-feeling towards the manager. Captain Jack Stephens said this month they are ‘fully behind’ Eckert.

The robustness of those alliances will be tested in due course, and ditto the party line repeated by many club sources that the squad has been galvanised through the turmoil. It is theoretically plausible, of course.

They wouldn’t be the first outfit to benefit from a siege mentality, which seemed to be the message of club CEO Phil Parsons when speaking at the same forum as Eckert. His soundbite: ‘We seem to be that club everybody hates this year, and I don't really care.’

The sentiment among supporters in the coming months will be fascinating. Much like the club, they want to forget a damaging, costly episode, but many have leant into their circumstances. When Eckert’s side played Colchester in the Carabao Cup first round last weekend, there were chants of: ‘We are Southampton, we'll spy when we want.’

As ever, the test of humour will come if results settle into a negative trend.

‘I think we're all coming to terms with what happened now and ready to move on,’ says Martin Starke, host of the popular Total Saints Podcast.

‘To be honest, I thought the manager would go and, at the time, I thought he should have. I was very angry about it, like a lot of people – we had tickets for Wembley and it was taken from underneath us. But I've mellowed a bit over the summer. We have to draw a line under it.

Even if Eckert survives, the pressure is considerable – the 2026-27 season is Southampton’s last under the comfort of parachute payments

Whatever Eckert delivers for his unwritten pages, it seems unlikely that he can muster an ending as wild as what has gone before. Assuming he gets the chance

‘I still don't think the punishment fitted the crime but moving forward we’re in a good situation – we're going into the season with a manager and a squad that has been together for a bit of time and proven they can win games in this league and perform. There are plenty of reasons to be positive.’

Eckert’s immediate future stands as a caveat to some of those points. Even if he survives, the pressure is considerable – the 2026-27 season is Southampton’s last under the comfort of parachute payments. ‘Now or never,’ as Starke put it.

Those financial imperatives were possibly illuminated by reported cuts to the women’s team set-up this summer, though an academy job has been offered to William Salt, the 23-year-old intern pressured into spying right back at the start of a scandal.

The image of him beside a tree, aiming his phone at a Middlesbrough training session, was the most surreal point of an extraordinary plot. Whatever Eckert delivers for his unwritten pages, it seems unlikely that he can muster an ending as wild as what has gone before. Assuming he gets the chance.

Sports.title: Everton forward charged by FA after allegedly breaking betting rules by placing 61 bets over 15 months
Sports.content:
Everton forward charged by FA after allegedly breaking betting rules by placing 61 bets over 15 months

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Everton forward Martin Sherif has been charged by the FA for allegedly breaching betting rules.

The 20-year-old, who was loaned out to Rotherham by the Toffees last season, has been accused of betting 61 times on matches over 15 months.

The bets allegedly were placed between November 20 in 2024 and February 12 in 2026 and Sherif now has until next Monday to respond to the charges.

The FA said in a statement: 'Martin Sherif of Everton FC has been charged with breaching the FA's betting rules.

'It's alleged that the player breached FA Rule E1.2 in respect of 61 bets placed on football matches between 20 November 2024 and 12 February 2026.

'Martin Sherif has until Monday 17 August to provide a response.'

Martin Sherif, pictured playing for Everton in 2023, has allegedly breached betting rules

Sherif has never made a professional appearance for Everton but trained with the first team last year.

He has been with the club since the age of 13 and boasted an impressive scoring record at youth level.

He scored twice in 10 games for Rotherham in League One last season but the loan was cut short in December by the Premier League side due to Sherif suffering a number of injuries.

The Liberia-born forward later joined Port Vale on loan in February but could not help them avoid relegation to League Two, scoring twice in 17 matches.

Sports.title: Chelsea sign Marc Cucurella replacement, Aston Villa line up move for West Ham star while Newcastle press on with pursuit of Benfica defender: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Chelsea sign Marc Cucurella replacement, Aston Villa line up move for West Ham star while Newcastle press on with pursuit of Benfica defender: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Palace set to sell another youngster

Belgian top-flight side Cercle Brugge are working on a six-figure deal to sign Tayo Adaramola from Crystal Palace.

The 22-year-old Palace academy product is in the final year of his contract, having spent six loan spells away from the club since 2022 and impressed at Sheffield Wednesday in the second half of last season.

Adaramola made his senior international debut this year, starting in the Republic of Ireland’s 5-0 win over Grenada in May.

He is expected to become the third academy player sold this summer, with Mofe Jemide set to join Alverca after Danny Imray joined Wrexham for £5million.

EXCLUSIVE BY BOBBY MANZI

Chelsea sign Marc Cucurella replacement

Chelsea have signed Rayo Vallecano left-back Pep Chavarria on a five-year deal for a fee of around £16.3m plus add-ons.

The 28-year-old replaces Marc Cucurella, who signed for Real Madrid earlier this summer in a £55.8m deal.

After signing his five-year deal, Chavarria told club media: 'I'm so excited to get started.

'This is a dream for me as Chelsea are one of the biggest clubs in the world. This is one of the best days of my life,' added the 28-year-old.

'It is a big opportunity but I am prepared and will work hard to help the team achieve success.

'There are a lot of people who have helped me get to this moment and I have to thank my family. They have always supported me and today is only possible because of them.'

Chelsea have signed Rayo Vallecano left-back Pep Chavarria on a five-year deal

Toon press on with Benfica target

Newcastle United are pressing ahead with talks to sign Amar Dedic from Benfica.

The 23-year-old right-back played for new Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle at RB Salzburg.

Dedic has been capped 31 times by Bosnia and is valued around £25m.

Newcastle continue to work on a new midfielder too.

Camara never lies

Crystal Palace have held further talks with Monaco over 22-year-old midfielder Lamine Camara.

The clubs have been discussing a £40million deal for the Senegal international who has also been tracked by Chelsea, Newcastle and Manchester United.

Camara impressed in Monaco's friendly against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

Monaco are understood to want a fee in excess of £50m for the midfielder who has three years left on his contract.

Palace have also spoken about France international Youssouf Fofana who is available from AC Milan.

Villa Wan him

Aston Villa are discussing a move for West Ham right-back Aaron Wan-Bissaka.

The 28-year-old is ready to leave West Ham to stay in the top flight and has been considered as a new addition by a number of clubs including Arsenal but Villa are understood to be in pole position.

The Congo international has also been linked with Everton but manager David Moyes is exploring other options.

Aston Villa are discussing a move for West Ham defender Aaron Wan-Bissaka

Villa are in the process of signing Matteo Ruggeri from Atletico Madrid to strengthen their left back options and now Wan-Bissaka looks a strong option for their right-back berth.

They have previously discussed Emerson Royal at Flamengo.

The Eagle has landed... again!

Evann Guessand has rejoined Crystal Palace on a season-long loan from Aston Villa.

Guessand spent the second half of last season on loan at Selhurst Park, playing 14 times as Palace won the UEFA Conference League.

Palace chose not to exercise his option to buy at the end of last season’s loan but remained open to the possibility of Guessand returning on loan. This switch also includes an option to buy.

Palace initially chased the Ivorian on a permanent deal last summer, but he opted to join Aston Villa - where he made just 21 appearances - in a £30million deal from Nice.

Rejoining Palace, Guessand said: ‘I'm so happy to be here. I already have good memories here – but I think it's only the beginning. I hope many more are coming.’

BOBBY MANZI

Spurs youngster heading to Belgium

Tottenham winger Yang Min-Hyeok has joined KVC Westerlo in Belgium on loan for the 2026/27 season.

Yang, 20, signed for Spurs in July 2024 but completed the season in South Korea and moved to London in January 2025. He has been on loan at QPR, Portsmouth and Coventry.

Spurs have a close relationship with Westerlo. Alfie Devine and Luka Vuskovic are among those who have been loaned there.

MATT BARLOW

City land Geronimo

Manchester City have signed goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli from Marseille for £1.7million.

The 34-year-old Argentina international has signed a two-year deal and provides cover after James Trafford was sold to Leeds for £40m plus £5m in add ons.

Rulli spent the 2016-17 season at City without making a first-team appearance, playing on loan at Real Sociedad.

Manchester City have signed goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli from Marseille for £1.7million

Till Douath do us part

Hull City have agreed a deal with RB Salzburg to sign midfielder Lucas Gourna-Douath in a permanent move worth £3.5m.

The 23-year-old is travelling to Hull for a medical.Sunderland had also shown interest.

The France U21 international has one year left on contract at Salzburg and impressed in the second half of last season with a spell on loan at Le Havre where he was instrumental in them avoiding relegation.

Wolf at the door for Jordan James

Wolves are closing on a £10million deal for Rennes midfielder Jordan James.

The 22-year-old Wales international had interest from Middlesbrough and West Ham also.

He impressed on loan at Leicester City last season scoring 11 goals in 34 games.

James first shot to prominence when he started out at neighbouring Birmingham City.

Munoz not Moyes' type

Everton manager David Moyes is an admirer of Crystal Palace’s Daniel Munoz but would prefer a more orthodox right-back rather than a wing-back.

Munoz could become available after Palace moved for 21-year-old winger and wing-back Anan Khalaili from Belgian club Union Saint-Gilloise.

The Israel international completed his medical at the weekend ahead of signing a five-year contract.

Flo no-go for Spurs

Tottenham maintain they are not pursuing a deal for Monaco’s former Arsenal striker Folarin Balogun.

Spence's Italian job

Tottenham and Inter Milan are in the final stages of negotiations over the sale of Djed Spence.

Inter have made an offer worth around £26.9million.

The 26-year-old emerged as a target for the Serie A champions prior to the World Cup but his performances for England convinced Inter further.

They initiated contacts in June for him, teammate Cristian Romero and free agent John Stones.

The latter has already joined and Inter also want to add Liverpool's Curtis Jones.

Talks for Spence advanced this morning and the fee is around £26.9m plus £4m in add-ons and a 10percent sell on.

Spence has agreed to the move and is waiting for permission to travel.

The defender previously enjoyed time in Italy while on loan with Genoa for six months from January 2024.

Inter have also agreed a deal to send Davide Frattesi on loan to Lazio with an obligation to buy at £11m. They hope that deals gives them room to buy Jones from Liverpool but they will have to meet Liverpool's valuation which has been £35m. Their last offer via intermediaries was considerably short of that.
