Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: 8-year-old boy reels in bizarre surprise during weekend fishing trip at Pennsylvania lake
World.content:
An 8-year-old boy went fishing for bass and catfish in Pennsylvania over the weekend and instead hauled in something that belongs roughly 4,000 miles farther south.

A piranha.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Seamus Coffey was fishing with his dad, Michael, at Ridley Park Lake on Saturday when something grabbed his line. At first, Seamus figured he had hooked a bass.

"I'm reeling it in, and I think there's a bass," Seamus told 6ABC Philadelphia.

His dad could tell pretty quickly, though, that this was not one of their usual catches.

"I was like, 'Slow down dude, you might lose it.' This looks like something we haven't caught before," Michael recalled.

Once the fish hit dry land, Dad was still trying to figure out what exactly they were looking at.

Seamus, meanwhile, apparently needed about three seconds.

"He said, 'It's a piranha!'" Michael said.

How did he know that?

"Because I watch YouTube!" Seamus said.

Michael pulled up photos on Google and came to the same conclusion, and the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission later confirmed that the roughly 9.5-inch, 2-pound fish was indeed some species of piranha.

Piranhas are native to South America, not suburban Philadelphia, so state officials have a pretty good idea how this one arrived at Ridley Park Lake: Somebody likely dumped a pet they no longer wanted.

Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission spokesperson Mike Parker said exotic animals can seem like a great idea when they're small, only for owners to eventually realize that housing, feeding and caring for them can become expensive and difficult.

Dumping them into a nearby lake, however, is not the solution.

"That is probably the worst thing you can do for an animal that's been a pet," Parker said.

It's also illegal. Pennsylvania prohibits releasing exotic species into the wild, and violators can face fines or prosecution.

Michael said he initially returned the fish to the water before reconsidering and ultimately disposed of it humanely. Parker said removing it was the right call because a non-native fish could pose a risk to people and disrupt the local ecosystem.

LARGEMOUTH BASS EXPLODES FROM WATER TO EAT CHARL SCHWARTZEL'S GOLF BALL AT LIV GOLF NEW YORK

Parker said this particular fish likely wouldn't have survived long outside its natural habitat anyway, especially after presumably spending its life as a pet.

And, bizarrely enough, Pennsylvania has been through this before.

In July 2016, a woman and her son hooked a red-bellied piranha at North Park Lake near Pittsburgh. That fish managed to flip back into the water after the anglers removed the hook. Officials at the time also suspected someone had released an unwanted aquarium fish and said Pennsylvania's cold weather would eventually take care of the problem.

Ten years later, another Pennsylvania kid has a piranha story of his own.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

And despite unexpectedly finding a mouthful of razor-sharp teeth on the end of his line, Seamus doesn't appear traumatized in the slightest.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"Fishing is my favorite thing," he said.

After Saturday, though, it's going to be pretty tough for the next bluegill to impress him.

World.title: Peggy Flanagan was Minnesota's No 2 official as massive fraud scandal exploded under state's watch
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Minnesota's new Democratic nominee for Senate has baggage heading into the November election: the massive fraud scandal that rippled through the Land of 10,000 Lakes happened right under her nose.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan scored a major win for the insurgent progressive movement that's reshaping the Democratic Party from the outside on Tuesday, toppling the more moderate Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., in the process. But her role during the Minnesota fraud scandal has plagued her campaign, with both sides attacking her on the issue.

It became Craig's prime line of attack against her.

"The lieutenant governor, even as we sit here today, continues to take absolutely no accountability for any of the fraud issues, and she continues to blame the governor," Craig said during a debate with Flanagan on Minnesota Public Radio. "And I'm going to be honest: It's pissing me off."

PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE

During the campaign, Craig charged that Flanagan had largely shrugged off responsibility for the fraud scandal, despite having served alongside Walz as his No. 2 since the pair were first elected in 2018.

In an interview with the Minnesota Reformer, Flanagan said, "The governor has said that the buck stops with him, and he took the lead here," on the fraud scandal.

Notably, Flanagan did not mention fraud during her victory speech Tuesday night, instead focusing on hallmarks of her campaign thus far, such as vowing to "rip [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] apart" following the deadly shootings in Minnesota earlier this year.

Still, the scandal torpedoed Walz's re-election hopes, and Republicans plan to lean into it in the weeks leading up to Nov. 3.

HALL OF FAMER TONY DUNGY ENDORSES MICHELE TAFOYA IN CROWDED MINNESOTA REPUBLICAN PRIMARY FOR U.S. SENATE

Her opponent, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, has already pounced on the opportunity several times this election season and did so again shortly after being crowned the Republican nominee for Senate.

"Minnesotans of every political stripe are fed up. They're exhausted with this fraud," Tafoya told a Minnesota Fox affiliate.

"We cannot show our children that failure comes without accountability," she continued. "We've got to have accountability, but more than that, we've got to do things, everything we do, to make Minnesota more livable, more affordable, more safe, and without fraud, and we're gonna do that."

National Republicans are confident that she could win big in November.

While Minnesota is not on the NRSC’s target map of eight battleground seats, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, believes Tafoya is a serious contender to Democrats, who have held both Senate seats since 2009.

"The one thing that gets me excited when I think about this election cycle on the map is Minnesota," Scott told CNN. "I think Minnesota, we have a real shot with Michele Tafoya."

REPUBLICANS GET THE DEMOCRAT THEY WANTED AS SOCIALIST ABDUL EL-SAYED WINS MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY

Republicans also see Tafoya’s more moderate leanings as a positive heading into November.

A GOP operative told Fox News Digital that she’s seen as a candidate who can unite swing, moderate and MAGA voters in a winning coalition.

"Tafoya has the power to appeal to a broader electorate that’s starving for authenticity," the operative said. "Her career as a sideline reporter for NBC’s ‘Sunday Night Football’ makes her relatable to a mainstream crowd."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Her position on abortion, for example, could attract swing voters.

In an open letter to Minnesotans, Tafoya wrote that, as a senator, she would oppose taxpayer-funded abortions, support conservative, strict-constructionist judges and remain "completely aligned with President Donald Trump on this issue." She also expressed support for the Dobbs decision.

But she won’t support a total ban on abortion.

"I do not support an outright ban on abortion, and I believe there should be reasonable access in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy," Tafoya wrote. "Further, I believe that states who restrict access to fertility treatments like IVF are also acting wrongly — being pro-family is pro-life."

World.title: Former 'Real Housewives' star calls Andy Cohen's political take defending 'MAGA' women 'full of s---'

Former "Real Housewives of Orange County" star Kelly Dodd claimed Bravo host Andy Cohen was "full of s---" Tuesday after he defended the inclusion of "MAGA women" on the show.

Dodd spoke to Fox News Digital after the "Watch What Happens Live" host was asked on Threads why there were "so many MAGA women" on the series, particularly the "Orange County" season.

"If we didn’t showcase people with different POV’s there would be no show. Also it’s a show about the women and their relationships, not about politics," Cohen wrote on Sunday.

KELLY DODD FIRES BACK AT CANCEL CULTURE, SAYS SHE'S TREATED LIKE 'AN OUTCAST' IN HOLLYWOOD

Dodd called out this comment, claiming Cohen and Bravo did not care for conservative perspectives on the show before and have since become concerned only about ratings.

"They're making excuses that they need points of view when I don't think that's true," Dodd said. "He doesn't have different points of view. I think he's full of s---."

Dodd pointed to Cohen's past comments attacking conservatives and right-leaning perspectives and viewed his Threads comment and described the suggestion that the show was welcoming different types of women as disingenuous.

"I think that he sees that the ratings are slipping, and he needs to get back some conservative. He's lost half of his audience. Any time you talk, speak about politics. ... you're gonna p--- off half the country," Dodd said.

ANDY COHEN BLASTS JOE ROGAN AS A 'F---ING IDIOT' AFTER HE BACKS PRATT FOR LA MAYOR

Cohen, however, agreed that the "Real Housewives" brand was not political in any way and that she had not discussed politics prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

"The show is not about politics. It's about women's lives. It's not about politics. No one's running for office,s or no one's talking about politics," Dodd said.

Bravo and its parent company NBCUniversal declined to comment.

Fox News Digital also reached out to Cohen's representative for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Dodd was among multiple women who were fired or left the franchise after making controversial comments or criticizing left-wing politics. Dodd was fired from the series in 2021 after controversial remarks about the COVID-19 pandemic and accusations of her mocking the Black Lives Matter movement.

REALITY STAR SAYS 'RHOC' COST HER MARRIAGE AS DAUGHTER SHUNS SHOW AFTER MILITARY HUSBAND'S PORTRAYAL

World.title: John Hinckley Jr gives his thoughts on Jodie Foster 45 years after shooting Ronald Reagan to impress her

John Hinckley Jr., the man who shot former President Ronald Reagan in 1981 to impress Jodie Foster, said he wants nothing but good things for the actress.

"I just wish Jodie Foster well," he said. "I don’t really see her movies, but I wish her well, and I know she’s doing quite well. And that’s all I can say: I just, I wish Jodie well, and I hope she has a good life."

The 71-year-old explained on the "Mark Joseph Show" in an exclusive preview shared with Entertainment Weekly that when he shot Reagan 45 years ago in a delusional state, he believed he would spend the rest of his life with the "Silence of the Lambs" actress.

REAGAN SHOOTER CALLS LINK TO WASHINGTON HOTEL ‘SPOOKY’ AFTER ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AT SAME SITE

The full episode will air on Wednesday.

"I wanted to have like this union with Jodie Foster and live the rest of my life with her and all these things that, of course, were delusional, but I was believing those things at that time. So, the best outcome would have been to just have like this union with Jodie Foster," Hinckley told Joseph after the host asked what he believed at the time would be the best thing that could come out of the shooting.

He explained that he believed at the time that Foster would "join me wherever I was. You know, I didn’t know if I was going to be in jail or hospital or what, but after things settled down, I had this notion that she was going to join me wherever I was."

It came out shortly after Hinckley’s assassination attempt that left Reagan with a broken rib, punctured lung and internal bleeding, that Hinckley was obsessed with Foster after seeing her in "Taxi Driver" and thought the shooting would make her notice him.

JODIE FOSTER HAUNTED BY HORRIFIC DOG TRAGEDY, BELIEVES SHE GAVE UP WHAT SHE LOVES MOST FOR SUCCESS

Hinckley was found not guilty by reason of insanity after shooting the former president outside the Washington Hilton two months after he was elected.

Former White House press secretary James Brady was shot in the head and suffered brain damage and partial paralysis, which led to his death in 2014. His death was ruled a homicide.

Two other men were also wounded in the shooting.

Hinckley was committed to a psychiatric hospital after the trial and released in 2016. By 2022, he was living in Virginia without any court restrictions.

Hinckley admitted to Joseph, however, that, in his delusional state, Foster could have been a target herself.

"She definitely could have been a target. It’s just fate went the other way," Hinckley said. "But, yeah, she could have been a target. But, as fate turned out, it was Reagan instead of her."

"I shot four people, and I’m sorry to the Reagan family, the Brady family, the other families of the victims," he said at the time. "I’m sorry to Jodie Foster for bringing her into this."

World.title: Mamdani's team said NYPD would accompany his wife on Middle East vacation — cops say that's not true

The New York Police Department (NYPD) will not provide a security detail to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's wife during her upcoming vacation to two terror hotspots in the Middle East, despite the mayor's office claiming otherwise.

"The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level 4 travel advisories for discretionary reasons such as personal travel," a spokesperson for the law enforcement agency told Fox News.

Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, is planning to travel to Syria and Lebanon to visit family in September, according to the New York Post. Both of those countries are on the State Department's "Do Not Travel" list due to terrorism concerns.

MAMDANI'S WIFE CO-HOSTS LUXE MUSLIM RETREAT CASTING VIRGIN MARY AS ‘PALESTINIAN WOMAN’ UNDER OCCUPATION

"Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the first lady’s security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon," Mamdani’s spokeswoman Dora Pekec reportedly said.

But later, as it became clear that the NYPD would not be making the overseas trek, the mayor chalked the confusion up to a staff "miscommunication" when asked about it by news outlet PIX11 on Tuesday.

NYPD Detectives’ Endowment Association (DEA) President Scott Munro furiously slammed the implication that NYPD detectives would accompany the city's First Lady to the Middle East.

MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS

"Our detectives put themselves in harm’s way every day protecting New Yorkers," said Munro. "The DEA would never remain silent if our members were asked to travel to a dangerous, off-limits foreign country for anything other than a legitimate law-enforcement or intelligence operation."

"Our detectives are needed here in New York City protecting residents and fighting crime," he added.

Mamdani has a long history of trashing the very police department he thought would accompany and provide security for his wife to the dangerous Middle Eastern countries on New York City taxpayer's dime.

"There is no negotiating with an institution this wicked & corrupt. Defund it. Dismantle it. End the cycle of violence," Mamdani said in reference to the NYPD in a viral 2020 post on X.

"We don't need an investigation to know that the NYPD is racist, anti-queer & a major threat to public safety," he said in another 2020 post, adding in a follow-up: "What we need is to #DefundTheNYPD."

JON STEWART PRESSES MAMDANI ON WHERE HE BREAKS WITH FELLOW DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ON PRISONS AND BORDERS

"Queer liberation means defund the police," he said in yet another post.

The mayor, who has also faced scrutiny for his anti-Israel views and recently called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" while calling for his arrest, derogatorily linked the NYPD to the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF).

"We have to make clear that when the boot of the NYPD is on your neck, it’s been laced by the IDF," Mamdani, who was a keynote speaker, said during a panel discussion at the Democratic Socialists of America's 2023 national convention.

During his campaign for mayor of the most populated U.S. city, Mamdani said the exact opposite, explicitly stating that he did not want to defund the police.

Still, it appears there is no love lost between Mamdani and the NYPD.

Just last week, he was booed offstage when he tried to speak at a pro-police event in Staten Island.

World.title: Alex Rodriguez defends Dodgers' spending spree as likely lockout gets closer: 'I think it's great'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

With a lockout more likely than not at this point in Major League Baseball, the ongoing debate continues over whether the Los Angeles Dodgers are actually ruining the sport.

Many believe the Dodgers have simply broken baseball, particularly with Shohei Ohtani's $700 million contract, 97% of which is deferred. They have won back-to-back World Series titles and are the favorite for a third consecutive title.

Not only did Los Angeles follow up its titles by signing the most touted reliever on the market in Edwin Diaz, but it also gave Kyle Tucker a deal that gave him the highest annual average value of $60 million, the most for any position player ever.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

However, former slugger Alex Rodriguez isn't buying the negativity surrounding the organization.

"I think it’s great. You and I both would be hypocrites if we said it’s not good when we saw what happened in the ‘90s here in New York, what happened in ‘09 when Hal Steinbrenner flexed his financial resources to go out and get [CC] Sabathia, [Mark] Teixeira and A.J. Burnett, and the year before we had Johnny Damon," A-Rod told New York Yankees broadcaster Michael Kay on the latter's radio show.

Rodriguez does make an interesting point — in 2005, the Yankees' payroll ($208.3 million, per Baseball Reference) was almost double the second-highest payroll (the Boston Red Sox's $123.5 million). The New York Mets ($101.3 million) were the only other team to have a nine-digit payroll.

While the Dodgers have finessed their contracts through deferrals and bonuses to make their actual payroll less than the actual value of the contracts, numerous other teams are actually still in the comparative ballpark. The Mets, Philadelphia Phillies and Toronto Blue Jays each have a tax payroll of at least $300 million.

Rodriguez noted that it's not necessarily the amount of money but how it's spent.

FORMER MLB STAR CALLS FOR SALARY FIX AS OWNERS, PLAYERS ASSOCIATION TALK 'TWO DIFFERENT LANGUAGES'

"The key is not making the mistakes..." Rodriguez said, name-dropping Trent Grisham and Ryan McMahon, who are combining to make $38 million this season while hitting a combined .215 with an OPS below .700.

"You have to be able to determine what is your inventory and what is it worth. Gene Michael used to be able to hold on to Bernie [Williams], [Derek] Jeter, [Jorge] Posada. That's the key — you got to hold on to your early guys, and then move on for the others, use them as assets to complement your current roster."

Again, to Rodriguez's point, the Milwaukee Brewers, whose $153 million tax payroll is 19th in the league, own the best record in Major League Baseball. The Tampa Bay Rays rank 27th in tax payroll yet have the league's second-best record, while the AL Central-leading Chicago White Sox rank 26th.

Furthermore, three of the top five payrolls in the sport — the Mets, Phillies and Blue Jays — are currently out of the postseason.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, and players have insisted they would not play under a salary cap, which has been formally offered for the first time since 1994.

World.title: Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman advance to GOP Senate primary runoff in South Carolina
World.content:
Appointed Sen. Darline Graham was forced into a Republican Senate primary runoff by Rep. Ralph Norman on Tuesday, raising the prospect that GOP voters will again reject a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump.

Graham, who was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham’s term in July, is looking to also take his place on the November ballot for a full six years in the Senate. Trump encouraged her to run and then endorsed her in a primary that featured 10 GOP candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry and former Gov. Mark Sanford.

Rep. Ralph Norman in the U.S. Capitol in March. Tom Williams / Getty Images

The winner of the Aug. 25 runoff will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a doctor who won her party’s primary in June.

Graham, the first woman ever to represent South Carolina in the Senate, has never held elected office before, and her thin résumé appeared to cost her with some voters in the first round of the primary, calling into question the power of Trump’s imprimatur.

“I understand that she’s lost a brother and lost someone very special to her, and I sympathize with that, but at the same time, I don’t think that it’s necessary just to give it to her,” Republican voter Bob Howell told NBC News in Lexington, South Carolina.

Asked about Trump endorsing Graham, Howell said, “I like President Trump, but I don’t think that that’s necessarily what sways my vote.”

Earlier this year, Trump’s favored candidate for governor, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, got pushed into a runoff against state Attorney General Alan Wilson. Trump then issued a rare dual endorsement of both candidates in the Republican primary runoff, which Wilson won. That was one of several races across the country this year in which Trump’s preferred candidate failed to win the Republican nomination for a high office.

The winner of this Republican runoff will be heavily favored to prevail in November in a state where a Democrat has not won a Senate seat since Fritz Hollings’ re-election in 1998.

Graham, 62, replaced her older brother in the Senate after Lindsey Graham died July 11, after emergency personnel responded to a “cardiac arrest” call at his Capitol Hill home. The elder Graham had been seeking a fifth term in November and had already won a competitive primary in June.

Trump wasted little time in throwing his weight behind the younger Graham, issuing his “complete and total endorsement” on Truth Social on July 17, less than a week after her brother’s death.

Rep. Russell Fry in Charleston. Bill Clark / Getty Images

In her brief tenure in the Senate, Graham has been centrally involved in one issue: passage of a measure, earlier this month, that would impose new sanctions on Russia and Iran. Lindsey Graham had been the chief proponent of an earlier version of the legislation, which focused on applying pressure to Russia. At Trump’s request, Iran provisions were added before the Senate renamed the measure for Lindsey Graham and passed it, 86-11.

“I think I’ve accomplished a whole lot in three weeks,” Graham said after she cast her vote Tuesday, pointing to the sanctions bill and her vote to confirm Attorney General Todd Blanche. “I’m not being handed the seat. I realize that I have to earn votes, so I’m working really hard to do that.”

Graham added that she expected the race to move to a runoff.

Norman, who finished a distant third in the state’s Republican gubernatorial primary earlier this year, consistently supports Trump’s agenda in Congress. But Lindsey Graham was one of the president’s closest allies — Trump eulogized the late senator during a service at Washington National Cathedral — and that loyalty was reciprocated in the endorsement of Graham.

Now, with most of the state’s Republican voters having cast ballots for her rivals, Graham will need to consolidate support quickly in order to keep a seat that has been in her family since 2003.

World.title: Minnesota GOP picks Lisa Demuth over Trump-backed Mike Lindell for governor against Democrat Amy Klobuchar
World.content:
Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth won the Republican primary for governor, NBC News projects, defeating Trump ally Mike Lindell and setting up a general election matchup against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Demuth’s victory was an upset over Lindell, the MyPillow founder and election conspiracy theorist. Lindell had been leading in limited public polling heading into Election Day, and President Donald Trump endorsed him.

But attacks on Lindell from fellow Republicans — including questions about his residency raised by the chairman of the Minnesota Republican Party — hampered his campaign in the final weeks before the primary, as members of the Minnesota GOP sought a nominee who could beat Klobuchar in the general election.

Mike Lindell at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, N.D., on July 1. Leigh Vogel / Getty Images

Lindell has faced several legal challenges since 2020, when he championed Trump’s debunked theories about the 2020 presidential election, which former President Joe Biden won.

At a Minnesota Farmfest forum this month, Klobuchar appeared alongside three GOP candidates for governor and accused each of them of being “a rubber stamp of Donald Trump.”

Demuth and other Republicans — including Trump — have attacked Democrats in the blue state over two sprawling fraud scandals involving Medicaid and pandemic aid. Among the allegations were that hundreds of millions of dollars that had been earmarked for welfare programs were stolen.

At the farm event, Demuth blamed “incompetent Democrat control” for the fraud cases, and she has pointed on the campaign trail to the Fraud Prevention Agency Oversight Committee, which she established leading the state House.

In January, Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, who had planned to run for a third term, decided to drop his re-election campaign, citing the attacks over the fraud cases. A few weeks later, Klobuchar launched her campaign. She is one of four senators to run for governor this year.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., at the U.S. Capitol in May. Heather Diehl / Getty Images

Still, Republicans will have to overcome political trends in Minnesota in November to win the Governor’s Residence. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by about 4 percentage points in the most recent presidential election, when Walz was her running mate.

World.title: Democratic Rep. John Larson loses his primary to opponent calling for generational change
World.content:
Democratic Rep. John Larson of Connecticut has lost his primary race to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, NBC News projects, becoming the latest example of Democratic voters’ push to sweep out incumbent House members and replace them with younger leadership.

See live results here

Larson, 78, has been a fixture in Connecticut politics, having served for more than a decade in the state Legislature and almost three decades in Congress. A former member of party leadership, he touted his work on Social Security in Congress and had been backed by the state’s congressional delegation, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and key unions.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin speaks in July. Jessica Hill / AP

But Bronin, 47, mounted a serious campaign against him, calling for generational change and arguing that President Donald Trump’s second term called for new energy and new direction from Democratic lawmakers. Bronin raised more money than Larson and won over party activists at the state convention, winning the state party’s endorsement.

Larson is the 10th House member to lose a primary this year: seven Democrats and three Republicans.

“In this moment, when Donald Trump is president, the job of a member of Congress isn’t just in the subcommittee rooms, it’s what you are doing outside the walls of the Capitol to build a movement,” Bronin said in a late May interview.

“Over these next two years, it’s so important to have Democratic members of Congress using that platform not just to give red-faced speeches to an empty chamber for the C-SPAN cameras, but to ... carry our message, to win people back who lost faith in our party.”

Congressman John Larson exits a press conference at the Legislative Office Building, March 6, 2026, Hartford, Ct. Mark Mirko / Connecticut Public Broadcasting / Getty Images

Asked Monday on NBC News’ “Meet the Press Now” about the movement for generational change in the Democratic Party, Larson said that “I think the change that we need is to continue to go after Donald Trump” and touted his “record of doing that.”

“I have the endorsement of more elected officials, every sitting member in the congressional delegation, because they understand what I’ve been able to deliver,” he said. “They understand that they’re able to work with me, and they understand what I’ve been able to accomplish on their behalf. Luke Bronin has no record. I’m running on a record of accomplishment and achievement.”

Bronin replied that Larson has been in office “for about 50 years, and for the last 10 years or so, I just think he’s gotten stuck in a routine. And I understand, you know, it’s hard to find anybody who does the same thing for 30 years and doesn’t get a little bit stuck in the routine, but this is not a moment that we can keep doing the same thing.”

World.title: Los Angeles Lakers sold to Bob Iger, Josh Kushner for $12 billion
World.content:
The Los Angeles Lakers are being sold to an ownership group led by Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, the businessmen confirmed to NBC News on Wednesday.

The deal for the storied franchise had a $12.5 billion price tag, two people familiar with the matter said.

“As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world,” they said.

“We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss. Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles.”

ESPN first reported the sale.

The Lakers were previously sold to businessman Mark Walter in October 2025 for a valuation of approximately $10 billion.

“Owning the Los Angeles Lakers has been one of the great honors of my life,” Walter said in a statement. “It has been an extraordinary investment, but what I will carry with me is the community, the fans, and a city that treats this team as family. I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players, and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter. The Lakers belong to Los Angeles, and I have every confidence the best is still ahead.”

The Lakers are one of the most iconic franchises in sports with 17 championships, most recently in 2020. Last season, the team finished fourth in the Western Conference before being eliminated by the Oklahoma City Thunder in the semifinals.

NBA superstar LeBron James, the all-time leading scorer in the league, played eight seasons in Los Angeles. He announced in July he was leaving to join the Philadelphia 76ers on a two-year, two-year, $8 million contract. The team will now be led by six-time NBA All-Star Luka Dončić, who was No. 1 the league with 33.5 points per game last season.

Kushner is the founder of venture firm Thrive Capital, co-founder of Oscar Health and a minority owner of the NBA’s Miami Heat. FIFA wanted to sell a minority stake in the World Cup to Thrive Capital, but the plan was halted amid worldwide backlash from soccer leaders in Europe, North America and Asia.

Kushner is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Iger is an American media executive who was CEO of the Walt Disney Co. from 2005 to 2020 and from 2022 to 2026. Iger and his wife, Willow Bay, are the majority owners of Angel City FC, a National Women’s Soccer League franchise based in Los Angeles. Their controlling stake was purchased in 2024 at a $250 million valuation.

Zach Nunn, who is being challenged by Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott in Iowa's 3rd Congressional District. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is running for U.S. Senate against Democrat Josh Turek.

World.title: Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy jury hearing from mental health counselor
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's trial entered a 12th day Wednesday. The jury is hearing testimony from Latiesha Dukes, a mental health counselor who worked with Clancy.

Dukes, who worked at the time for South Shore Hospital, first met with Clancy in late November 2022 into early December of that year. She met with Clancy four times total during that time.

You can watch the trial in Plymouth Superior Court live on CBS News Boston in the embedded video or on YouTube when court is in session.

Clancy, 36, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. She has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham said Clancy planned the murders and faked a suicide attempt.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said Clancy admits to killing her children but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Witness Latiesha Dukes, a mental health clinician, testifies during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Mental health counselor takes witness stand

Dukes said she worked closest on Clancy's case with Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who finished her testimony on Tuesday.

"Her presenting concerns were anxiety, lack of sleep, suicidal ideation, thoughts of no longer wanting to live or be here," Dukes said.

Dukes testified that her feeling about Clancy's diagnosis was postpartum anxiety because she did not have anxiety about most things. She recommended outpatient therapy, continued use of medications, and seeing her for weekly therapy.

On Dec. 5, 2022, Clancy reported that she had a difficult weekend and had intrusive thoughts about wanting to die.

Following her meeting with Clancy that day, Dukes said she recommended partial hospitalization.

On Dec. 19, 2022, Dukes said Clancy seemed more engaged during a telehealth visit, was able to smile and laugh and was enjoying time with her family.

Dukes testified that on her last visit with Clancy, she seemed to show an improvement of mood and ability to connect with others. She said that Clancy did not show signs of mania, delusions, paranoia or psychosis.

On cross-examination, Reddington asked about Clancy's reluctance to take medications.

"She was concerned about becoming addicted to medication, yes," Dukes said.

Massachusetts State Police investigator testifies

Earlier, Sgt. Dan Lawlor testified. Lawlor has worked for Massachusetts State Police for nine years.

The night of the children's deaths, Lawlor went to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth and saw Clancy, who was unable to speak and suffering from injuries after jumping out a second-floor window.

Lawlor went to Boston Children's Hospital to check on 8-month-old Callan's status, then later went to Brigham and Women's Hospital, where Clancy was transferred, to stand watch outside the room.

Reddington took over cross-examination after about 15 minutes. The defense attorney asked Lawlor about how no one was allowed to get into Clancy's hospital room. Eventually, Reddington got a court order for psychologist Paul Zeizel to enter the room to meet with Clancy.

"Isn't it fair to say that one of the contentions of the district attorneys is that Paul Zeizel, my doctor, that I got a court order to get in and see her, told her to call Pat and tell him that she heard voices?" Reddington asked.

When Reddington referred to Pat, he was speaking about Patrick Clancy. Lindsay and Patrick Clancy were married at the time of their children's deaths, but have since divorced.

Following that question, the judge asked to see attorneys at sidebar due to an objection by the prosecution. After about 20 minutes, the judge sent jurors out of the room to question Lawlor without the jury present.

With the jury out of the room, Reddington asked about Lawlor's recollection that lead investigator Josh McKelligan had told him that at some point when Clancy was hospitalized, she called Patrick to indicate she was hearing voices. Reddington suggested that the theory investigators were trying to use was that Zeizel had suggested Clancy make the phone call.

"I don't know if it's a theory or not, I just recall the conversation," Lawlor said.

The prosecutor then questioned Lawlor without the jury present.

"You never had a conversation with the prosecution about what the theory was, did you?" she asked. Lawlor said he had not, saying it was only with the fellow trooper.

"Is this conversation guiding your testimony?" Buckingham asked. Lawlor said it was not.

The judge took arguments under advisement and the jury returned a short time later.

With the jury back in the room, Reddington asked Lawlor if he and McKelligan talked about the theory that Zeizel "is the reason that she told her husband she heard voices." Lawlor said they did talk about that theory.

"There's no investigator basis for that, that's McKelligan's speculation, correct?" Reddington asked. Lawlor said that was correct.

Buckingham then questioned Lawlor.

"Is it fair to say you oftentimes will have conversations as investigations are unfolding with other investigators that you're working on the case with about the case, potential evidence, theories of the case?" Buckingham asked.

Lawlor said that was true, and added that theories can change over time.

Buckingham asked Lawlor, "You didn't hear anything that occurred in that room that day that you were there when Dr. Zeizel was there, did you?"

"I did not hear anything," Lawlor said, concluding his testimony at around 10:45 a.m.

Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Lindsay Clancy trial

The jury heard from a psychiatric nurse practitioner Tuesday who specializes in postpartum patients. Rebecca Jollotta said she met with Clancy three times late in 2022, a few weeks before the murders. Jollotta was the 62nd witness in the trial.

Judge William Sullivan said the attorneys told him the proceedings are "well on schedule and somewhat ahead of schedule."

If convicted of first-degree murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If the jury finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: NYC Council probes prediction markets over advertising practices
World.content:
The New York City Council said Wednesday that it is investigating four prediction markets over allegations that the companies engage in deceptive marketing.

The probe will examine the advertising practices of Gemini Titan, Kalshi and Polymarket, all of which are based in New York, as well as Texas-based Coinbase.

"Prediction markets aggressively entice consumers to bet and wager on sports, politics, culture, weather and pretty much anything," New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a statement. "We refuse to let New Yorkers, especially our young people, become collateral damage."

A Polymarket  in a subway station in New York on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

As part of the investigation, Menin has requested information from the platforms about their marketing practices in New York.

Prediction markets allow users to wager on sports, political elections and many other events.

A spokesperson for the New York City Council said the companies were selected based on public reports and other information it has examined as part of its ongoing investigation into the prediction market industry. The council also considered how much of the companies' marketing reaches New York City residents, the spokesperson said.

The inquiry could be expanded to include more platforms, the spokesperson added.

Polymarket allegations

The probe comes after a June investigation by the Wall Street Journal uncovered that Polymarket paid online content creators to post videos that misrepresented their earnings from trades. In response, the platform said it would conduct an audit of its promotional content.

On Monday, the New York City Council said it would also investigate these allegations against Polymarket, including claims that the company targets younger adults using false and deceptive marketing.

"The Council is investigating allegations involving Polymarket and, critically, the extent to which similar marketing practices are prevalent within the prediction market industry more broadly, and related social harms to City residents," Menin said in a letter addressed to Polymarket founder and Chief Executive Shayne Coplan that was shared with CBS News.

Menin, a city council member who represents the Upper East Side, said the ultimate goal of the investigation is to determine whether more legislation, enforcement and education are necessary to combat "abusive marketing" in New York City.

"We look forward to engaging with the New York City Council on this matter," Polymarket said in a statement.

A Coinbase spokesperson said in an email that the company "offers our customers access to federally regulated prediction markets overseen by the CFTC, and fully complies with applicable laws."

The other companies subject to the investigation didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

New York City's probe highlights the broader turf battle between states and the federal government over who should have regulatory control over prediction markets. Multiple states have filed lawsuits against the platforms, including New York, where Attorney General Letitia James has sued Coinbase, Gemini Titan and Kalshi, accusing them of running illegal gambling operations that flout state laws.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets, has filed lawsuits seeking to block states from tightening rules governing them. The agency argues that Congress gives it exclusive jurisdiction over the regulation of derivative markets.

Yet attorneys note that it remains legally murky whether the CFTC's jurisdiction extends to sports betting, which drives much of the trading volume on prediction markets.

The city council's investigation that was announced Wednesday doesn't focus on whether prediction markets' practices violate state gambling laws, according to Menin's letter to Polymarket.

World.title: What happens after you miss three credit card payments?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Each credit card payment you miss will escalate the consequences you're facing in a specific, predictable way. KimberlyDeprey/Getty Images

Credit card balances are moving higher again, adding to the financial pressure on borrowers at a time when many are already struggling to keep up with their bills. Credit card balances increased by $21 billion nationwide during the second quarter of 2026, reaching $1.26 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest Household Debt and Credit Report, released this week. At the same time, 4.7% of all outstanding household debt was in some stage of delinquency, a clear indicator of how heavy borrowers' debt burdens have become.

For borrowers who have already fallen behind on their credit card payments, though, the bigger concern may be how quickly an individual account can progress from a simple late payment to a more serious financial problem. Missing one monthly payment can result in fees and credit score consequences, but falling behind for several billing cycles can create a much different situation, particularly as the overdue balance continues to grow and the account moves deeper into delinquency.

That makes the three-payment mark an important one to understand. By that point, the potential consequences can extend well beyond another late fee. So, what exactly happens after you miss three consecutive credit card payments, and what can you do if you've already reached that point? That's what we'll examine below.

Find out how you can start tackling your unpaid debt today.

What happens after you miss three credit card payments?

Each missed payment escalates the situation in a specific, predictable way. Here's what can happen if you miss three consecutive credit card payments in a row:

Your credit can take a significant hit

Credit card issuers can generally report an account as delinquent once it is at least 30 days past due. If you continue missing payments past that point, the account can subsequently be reported as 60 days and then 90 days late. That matters because payment history is an important factor in calculating your credit score. A series of missed payments can cause significant credit damage, and negative payment information can generally remain on your credit reports for up to seven years, so catching up on payments won't immediately erase the history of delinquency.

Learn what debt relief options you may qualify for now.

Your interest rate could increase

By the time you've missed three payments, another potentially expensive consequence can come into play: a higher credit card interest rate. Federal credit card rules generally restrict issuers from raising the rate on an existing balance simply because you've made a late payment, but an important exception applies when you hit the 60-day mark. At that point, the issuer may be able to apply a penalty rate to your existing balance, which can make it even more difficult to catch up. Interest is already accruing, and a higher credit card APR can increase the cost of the debt even further.

You could lose access to the card

Your available credit may also become less reliable as the delinquency progresses. Depending on the issuer and your circumstances, your card could be suspended or closed after missing payments, preventing you from making additional purchases. Losing access to the credit card doesn't eliminate the outstanding balance, though. You'll still be responsible for repaying what you owe even if you can no longer make purchases.

Collection efforts could become more serious

At roughly 90 days late, the account typically hasn't reached the standard charge-off point for credit card debt. That doesn't mean the issuer will simply wait for you to catch up, though. You may receive more frequent communications about the overdue balance, and the card issuer may escalate its internal collection efforts or offer options designed to get payments back on track. And, if the delinquency continues, the situation can become even more serious.

What debt relief options should you consider after three missed payments?

Three missed payments can be a sign that the problem has moved beyond an occasional cash-flow issue. If you don't have enough money to bring the account current — or if you're behind on multiple credit cards — it may be time to consider whether some form of debt relief could help.

Start by contacting your card issuer. Many issuers offer hardship programs that can temporarily reduce payments or interest rates, waive certain fees or otherwise make repayment more manageable. The earlier you ask about these programs, the more options you may have.

You can also consider credit counseling or a debt management plan if you can afford to repay your balances but need lower rates or a more structured repayment plan to facilitate it. Debt consolidation may also be worth exploring if you qualify for financing with a lower rate and can afford the new payment.

If you're facing true financial hardship and can't realistically repay your full unsecured debt balances, debt forgiveness, also known as debt settlement, may be another option to consider. With this route, the goal is to negotiate with creditors to settle the balance for less than what's owed. There are downsides, though, so make sure you consider all factors before moving forward.

The bottom line

Three missed credit card payments is a real turning point for your debt, not just a bad stretch. The account moves from a minor late payment problem to a serious delinquency issue with fees, credit score damage and collections activity attached. That means it's imperative that you take steps to resolve the issue, whether you do so by calling the issuer, enrolling in a hardship program, settling the account or speaking with a credit counselor about your options.
