What to Expect at the Yo Tomo Cafe Peruano festival Lima

Set in the Pasaje Los Pintores, the festival turns a familiar spot into an open-air coffee lab. This pedestrian walkway runs along the side of Parque Kennedy.

From 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., you’ll find dozens of stands. They represent eight regions: Ayacucho, Amazonas, Cusco, Junín, Pasco, Puno, San Martín, and Ucayali.

That’s not just a list of names. It’s a map of Peru’s altitude, climate, and soil, all in the cup.

Expect to taste a wide range of profiles. Cusco often brings bright, citrusy beans from the Quillabamba valley.

Junín, Peru’s largest coffee region, typically offers chocolatey, full-bodied brews. San Martín, in the high jungle, tends toward floral and fruity notes.

The festival is designed for comparison. Sip a washed process from Puno, then try a natural process from Amazonas.

See how the same bean reacts to different handling.

Beyond the Cup: Workshops, Contests, and Coffee Party

The organizers packed the schedule with more than tastings. There are brewing method demonstrations — pour-over, French press, siphon, and cold brew.

You can ask questions in Spanish or English, depending on the barista. Latte art contests happen throughout the weekend.

Baristas from Lima’s top cafes compete for bragging rights. You can watch, cheer, and maybe pick up a trick for your home setup.

Cultural presentations — often Andean music or dance — add a festive layer. Raffles give away bags of coffee and brewing gear.

The “Coffee Party” on the final evening is a casual gathering. Attendees mingle with producers over shared pots of coffee.

A DJ or live acoustic set often plays in the background. It’s a low-key way to end the weekend, and it’s all free.

Why This Matters for Expats and Nomads in Lima

For anyone in Latin America, coffee is more than a morning ritual. It’s an economic engine and a cultural connector.

Peru is one of the world’s top coffee exporters. Yet most of its best beans are shipped abroad, leaving locals with generic blends.

This festival is a direct counter to that trend. It connects you to the people who grow the coffee, not just those who sell it.

For expats, it’s also a practical networking opportunity. You’ll meet cafe owners, roasters, and importers looking for English-speaking collaborators.

They often need help with marketing, logistics, or content creation. Living in Lima means dealing with inconsistent quality.

This festival gives you a reliable reference point. Taste what good Peruvian coffee actually is, and learn the names of regions and producers.

Then seek those out in the city’s growing specialty cafe scene. It’s also a reminder that Peru’s diversity extends far beyond Machu Picchu.

Eight regions in one park is a crash course in geography. You get to drink your way through it.

Practical Tips for Attending the Yo Tomo Cafe Peruano festival Lima

Go early on a weekday if you can. Thursday and Friday mornings are quieter, so you’ll have more time to talk to producers.

Bring cash in soles — some vendors accept cards, but many small farmers prefer cash. Prices for bags typically range from 15 to 40 soles (US$4 to US$11).

Premium lots can go higher. Tastings are free, but pace yourself.

Drink water between samples.

Parque Kennedy is easy to reach by Metropolitano (the Estación Benavides stop is a short walk) or by taxi. If you’re driving, parking in Miraflores on a weekend is a challenge.

Consider ride-sharing or public transport. The festival runs rain or shine — August in Lima is winter, so bring a light jacket and expect overcast skies.

Remember: the event is free, but the coffee is not. Budget for a few bags to bring home, because you will want to.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Yo Tomo Cafe Peruano festival Lima really free? Yes, entry is completely free. All tastings, workshops, contests, and cultural presentations are included. You only pay if you buy coffee beans or food from the vendors. Where exactly is the festival held? It’s in the Pasaje Los Pintores, the pedestrian walkway on the side of Parque Kennedy in Miraflores. Look for the stalls and banners; you can’t miss it. Can I buy coffee to take home? Yes, most producers sell bags of their beans. Prices vary by region and quality, but expect to pay around 15 to 40 soles (US$4 to US$11) for a 250-gram bag. Some premium lots cost more.

Sources: Infobae Perú, Inforegión

For a city that rarely slows down, a Sunday morning in a green park is rare. No ticket price is attached.

It works for solo newcomers and families alike.

If you’re in São Paulo in mid-August and want a low-pressure way to meet people, move your body, and enjoy one of the city’s best green spaces, the Vamos Passear festival Sao Paulo is your answer. This isn’t a race to train for.

It’s a morning out with a 10 km bike ride, a 4 km walk, a kids’ run, and free activities.

You can show up, join in, or just watch and wander.

São Paulo’s Vamos Passear festival closes with a free day at Villa-Lobos. (Photo: Rudolph.A.furtado, Public domain)

What to Expect on the Day

The festival closes its 2026 season at Parque Villa-Lobos on Sunday, 16 August. The park is a favorite among expats and nomads in the western zone.

It’s big, flat, and full of joggers, cyclists, and families on weekends.

On this day, it gets a festival overlay. There are organized starts, music, and an arena to try something new without paying a cent.

The bike ride (10 km) kicks off at 7h30. The walk (4 km) follows at 8h30.

If you have kids aged 4 to 14, the Corrida Kids starts at 9h30. Distances range from 50 m to 400 m, depending on age.

The arena — with dance, yoga, pilates, sports, games, and children’s activities — runs alongside the events, all free.

You don’t need to be fit; you just need to show up.

Costs and Registration

Here’s the part that makes this a no-brainer: the arena activities are completely free. No ticket, no wristband, no hidden charge.

For timed events like the bike ride, walk, and kids’ race, registration may be required. Some organizers charge a small fee for logistics.

The research doesn’t confirm a specific price for the 2026 edition. Check official festival channels closer to the date if you plan to participate.

If a fee applies, it’s typically modest — think R$ 20–R$ 40 (US$ 4–US$ 8). But don’t treat that as a guarantee; it’s an estimate.

What’s certain is that you can attend, watch, and use the arena without spending anything. For a city where weekend brunch can run R$ 80 (US$ 15) per person, a free morning in a park is a genuine bargain.

Bring water, sunscreen, and comfortable shoes. São Paulo in August is dry and mild, with mornings that start cool and warm up quickly.

Why This Matters for Expats and Nomads

Living in Latin America often means figuring out how to build a community from scratch. A festival like this is a shortcut.

It’s not a networking event with name tags. It’s a shared, unpretentious experience.

Join a yoga class, cheer for a kid, or walk 4 km. That’s how you start to feel less like a visitor and more like a resident.

For digital nomads, it’s also a reminder that São Paulo has a softer side. The city is known for business, traffic, and nightlife.

But Parque Villa-Lobos offers trees, open sky, and a free community gathering.

If you’re weighing whether to stay in São Paulo long-term, days like this tip the scale. It’s the kind of event that makes a megacity feel human.

How to Get There and Make the Most of It

Parque Villa-Lobos is in the Alto de Pinheiros area, west of the center. The easiest way in is by car or ride-share — there’s parking, but it fills up early on event days.

If you prefer public transport, the park is a short walk from the Villa-Lobos–Jaguaré CPTM station, and several bus lines stop nearby. Aim to arrive by 7h00 to join the bike ride.

The walk starts later, so 8h00 gives you a relaxed buffer.

After the events, stay for the arena. Try a class, let the kids burn off energy, or just find a patch of grass and watch.

The festival wraps up by early afternoon, leaving you the rest of Sunday free. If you’re new to the city, scout the neighborhood.

Nearby Pinheiros and Vila Madalena have cafes, coworking spaces, and restaurants nomads love.

Make a day of it: festival in the morning, exploration in the afternoon.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Vamos Passear festival really free? Yes — the arena activities (dance, yoga, pilates, sports, games, and kids’ actions) are free for everyone. The timed events — bike ride, walk, and kids’ race — may require registration, and a small fee could apply. No price is confirmed for 2026, so check the official channels before registering. Do I need to register in advance? For the arena, no — just show up. For the bike ride, walk, or kids’ race, registration is likely required, and spots may be limited. Check the festival’s official website or social media in the weeks before 16 August for the registration link and any fee details. What should I bring? Comfortable shoes, water, sunscreen, and a hat. August in São Paulo is dry with mild mornings, so a light layer helps early on. If you’re biking, bring your own bike or check for rentals. Rentals are common at Villa-Lobos but not guaranteed for the event, so arrive early.

Sources: Contra Relógio

For expats and digital nomads, Cartagena Youth Week is a rare window into how the city invests in its next generation. It is also a chance to join local life beyond the walled city’s tourist circuit.

If you’re living in Cartagena this August, mark your calendar. The city’s biggest free youth event of the year is coming.

Cartagena Youth Week runs from August 12 to 15, 2026. It packs four days with sports, environmental clean-ups, a university and job fair, a live DJ set, and a 5K race.

All of it is at no cost. Whether you’re a digital nomad or an expat, this is your chance to plug into the community.

Meet locals or understand the city beyond tourist zones.

Four Days, One City: The Full Agenda

The week kicks off on Wednesday, August 12. The Rally enseña starts at 3:00 p.m. in Parque Espíritu del Manglar.

It’s a scavenger-hunt style event that blends city knowledge with teamwork. It’s a fun, low-pressure way to explore a lesser-known park and meet people.

No sign-up details have been confirmed. So show up early and ask around.

Thursday morning, August 13, shifts to the outdoors. A Jornada ambiental starts at 8:00 a.m. in the Bicentenario neighborhood.

Expect gloves, trash bags, and a group of volunteers cleaning up green spaces. It’s a hands-on way to give back to the city you call home.

It’s also a good chance to practice your Spanish with locals who care about their barrio.

Friday, August 14, is the centerpiece. The Festival de las Juventudes takes place at Plaza de Variedades from 5:00 p.m. onward.

Universities set up booths to showcase programs. Employment agencies share job openings.

A youth entrepreneurship fair highlights small businesses. The special guest is DJ JAC.

He will close the evening with a live set. This is the event to hit if you’re curious about studying, working, or starting a side project in Colombia.

Saturday, August 15, ends the week with the JovenRun 5K. It is also at Plaza de Variedades, but it starts at 5:00 a.m. Yes, it’s early.

But it’s also cooler and less crowded. The race is free and open to all paces.

So don’t worry about being competitive. Just bring water, wear light clothing, and enjoy the sunrise run through the city streets.

What’s On Through the Week

The week runs on daily themes. Wednesday’s Rally Enseña starts at 3 p.m. in the Parque Espíritu del Manglar.

Later days focus on jobs, entrepreneurship and the environment. Most sessions are outdoors and free to join.

The big night is Friday’s Festival de las Juventudes at the Plaza de Variedades. DJ JAC headlines the lineup.

Saturday closes with the JovenRun 5K, also at the Plaza de Variedades. It starts early, at 5 a.m.

Why Cartagena Youth Week Matters for Expats and Nomads

Living in Latin America as an expat or digital nomad often means floating between coworking spaces, beach bars, and Airbnb apartments. Events like Cartagena Youth Week are a reminder that the city is more than a backdrop for your remote work.

It’s a living, breathing place with its own priorities. And here, the city is investing heavily in its young people.

By attending, you’re not just a spectator. You’re participating in the social fabric.

You’ll see how local government engages with youth. You’ll see what issues matter, like jobs, environment, and education.

You’ll see how vibrant the community scene is outside the tourist bubble.

There’s also a practical angle. Thinking of staying longer, starting a business, or hiring locally?

The Friday festival connects you directly to universities and employment agencies.

You can network with young entrepreneurs. You can learn about local talent.

You can get a feel for the city’s economic pulse. And if you’re just here for a few months, the 5K and the environmental day are low-cost, high-reward ways to make friends.

They help you feel like you belong. Plus, all activities are free.

No local currency needed, so no conversion math required.

Practical Tips for Attending

First, plan your week around the two anchor events. Those are Friday’s festival and Saturday’s race.

The festival starts at 5:00 p.m. So you can spend the day working and then head over. The race, however, starts at 5:00 a.m. Set two alarms and prep your gear the night before.

For the environmental day on Thursday, wear closed-toe shoes and bring sunscreen. For the rally on Wednesday, bring your phone for photos and a curious mindset.

Second, follow the Mayor’s Office channels for the daily schedule and meeting points. These are likely to fill up fast.

The kayaking and snorkeling slots will go quickly. Follow Cartagena’s official social media or check local news sites in the days leading up to August 12.

If you miss out, don’t worry. The main events on the agenda require no reservation.

Just show up. Finally, remember that Cartagena in August is hot and humid.

Hydrate constantly, wear light clothing, and pace yourself. The city is rewarding those who show up.

And this week, showing up is completely free.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cartagena Youth Week really free? Yes, all activities listed are completely free. That includes the rally, environmental day, festival, and 5K. The the week spans sport, environment, jobs, entrepreneurship and culture. But they may require early arrival or prior registration through the Mayor’s Office. Do I need to register in advance for the JovenRun 5K? No registration has been announced. The race starts at 5:00 a.m. at Plaza de Variedades on August 15. Show up early, stretch, and join the starting line. If you want to be safe, check the city’s official channels a few days before. Look for any last-minute sign-up instructions. Are these events only for young people? The events are designed for the youth population. But they are open to everyone. Expats and nomads of any age are welcome to join. The festival’s university and employment booths are useful for anyone considering study or work in Colombia. The race and environmental day are community-wide activities.

Here’s what you need to know, how to plan for it, and why it’s worth your time. Even if you usually skip conferences.

What Is Colombia Tech Fest Bogota?

Colombia Tech Fest Bogota is the flagship event of Colombia Tech Week 2026. The festival runs on Thursday 13 and Friday 14 August, from morning to evening, at Parque Museo El Chicó.

The venue is a real park — think gardens, walking paths, and open lawns — not a convention center. That means you’ll be moving between outdoor stages and shaded areas.

The city’s usual Bogotá weather will be your backdrop. Bring a light jacket.

Mornings can be cool, and afternoons can surprise you.

The organizers describe it as a “festival,” not a conference. That distinction matters.

Expect a more relaxed vibe than a typical corporate tech summit. There will be speakers, but there will also be space to wander, talk, and actually meet people.

The full agenda and speaker list go live on colombiatechfest.co. Tickets are sold through La Tiquetera.

Prices haven’t been announced yet, so check the site closer to the date. For reference, similar two-day tech events in Bogotá usually land between COP$150,000 and COP$400,000 (roughly US$35 to US$95).

That’s an estimate, not a confirmed number.

How to Attend and What to Expect

Getting to Parque Museo El Chicó is straightforward. It’s located on Calle 7a and Carrera 11, in the Chicó neighborhood.

That area is well-connected by TransMilenio and ride-hailing apps. If you’re coming from Chapinero or Usaquén, a taxi or Uber will take about 15–20 minutes depending on traffic.

There’s limited parking, so public transit or a ride-share is your best bet. The park itself is small enough that you won’t be doing marathon walks between stages.

But you will be outside, so wear comfortable shoes.

For tickets, go directly to La Tiquetera’s website. Search for “Colombia Tech Fest.” Early-bird pricing, if offered, will likely be cheaper than door sales.

The festival is bilingual-friendly.

Many talks in Bogotá’s tech scene are in Spanish with English slides, and some are fully in English. If you’re still learning Spanish, don’t let that stop you.

The networking areas and demo zones are where the real value is. Those don’t require perfect language skills.

Bring business cards or a digital contact-sharing app, because you will meet people.

Why This Matters for Expats and Nomads

For anyone living in Latin America, this festival is a signal. Bogotá is positioning itself as a regional tech hub.

Events like this are how you tap into that community. As an expat or digital nomad, you’re not just a visitor.

You’re part of the local economy. Showing up to events like Colombia Tech Fest Bogota helps you build a professional network based in the city, not just online.

That matters for finding clients, collaborators, or even a co-founder who understands the local market.

It also matters because the open-air format lowers the barrier. You don’t need to be a startup founder or a CTO to attend.

You can be a freelancer, a remote worker, or someone curious about where the region’s tech is heading. Colombia Tech Week, which runs from 10 to 16 August, includes more than 250 events across multiple cities.

That means you can sample smaller meetups, workshops, and talks all week. Then you can cap it off with the main festival.

It’s a low-cost way to get a high-resolution picture of Colombia’s tech scene. You can also find your place in it.

Beyond the Festival: Colombia Tech Week

Don’t make the festival your only stop. Colombia Tech Week 2026 spans the entire week of 10–16 August.

Bogotá is the main hub, but there are events in other cities too. The 250+ events include hackathons, panel discussions, startup pitches, and community meetups.

Some are in coworking spaces, others in universities or parks. The full calendar is typically published on the official Tech Week site.

Many events require separate registration even if they’re free.

For a digital nomad, this week is a golden opportunity to go deep without committing to a long-term project. You can attend a morning workshop on AI tools.

You can catch an afternoon talk on fintech regulation. You can join an evening networking session.

All of that can happen in one day, all free. The festival itself is the anchor.

But the week around it is where you’ll find the niche communities: women in tech, blockchain enthusiasts, edtech founders, and more. Plan your week ahead, book your free spots early, and treat the whole thing as a crash course in Colombian innovation.

You’ll leave with more than swag. You’ll leave with contacts and context.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much do tickets cost? Official prices haven’t been published yet. Tickets will be sold via La Tiquetera. Based on similar Bogotá tech events, expect COP$150,000 to COP$400,000. That’s roughly US$35 to US$95 for a two-day pass. This is an estimate. Check colombiatechfest.co for confirmed pricing. Do I need to speak Spanish? No. Many talks are bilingual or have English materials. The networking areas are language-flexible, and you’ll find plenty of English-speaking attendees. Knowing some Spanish helps, but it’s not a requirement. Is the festival child-friendly or pet-friendly? The venue is a public park, so the space itself is open. However, the festival hasn’t announced specific family or pet policies. If you plan to bring kids or a dog, check the official site closer to the date for any restrictions.

World.title: Fonseca and Cerúndolo Drawn Into the Same Cincinnati Quarter
World.content:
The 2026 Cincinnati Open draws were released Tuesday, and Latin America’s two most prominent men landed in the same crowded section of the bracket. Brazil’s João Fonseca, seeded 23rd, and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, seeded 20th, were both placed in the third quarter headed by American Taylor Fritz, a section that also contains 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev, 2021 runner-up Andrey Rublev, Norway’s Casper Ruud, American Brandon Nakashima, Belgian Zizou Bergs and wildcard Marin Čilić, who won the tournament in 2016.

The two cannot meet before the quarterfinals. Both will have to survive a section stacked with former Masters 1000 winners to get there. The draw arrives under unusual circumstances. World Nos. 1 and 2 Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who won the last two men’s titles at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, are both absent, Sinner with a knee injury and Alcaraz with a wrist injury.

Their withdrawals leave the men’s field without the two players who have decided nearly every major hard-court event of the past two seasons. Alexander Zverev, the 2021 champion, acknowledged the shift in an assessment of the field, noting Sinner’s record streak of 34 consecutive Masters 1000 match victories and six titles this year.

“I think it does change things a little bit, especially with Jannik not being here,” Zverev said. “But for me, it doesn’t change much. I still want to compete against the best.” Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo, seeded 22nd, drew a different assignment. He was placed in Zverev’s quarter alongside Flavio Cobolli, the rising Spaniard Rafael Jodar, American Tommy Paul, Valentin Vacherot of Monaco, Belgian Alexander Blockx, Hubert Hurkacz and Denis Shapovalov.

Peru’s Ignacio Buse, seeded 29th at 21 years old, sits in the bottom quarter. That section is headed by second seed Félix Auger-Aliassime and includes Ben Shelton, Lorenzo Musetti, Americans Learner Tien and Frances Tiafoe, France’s Ugo Humbert and Arthur Rinderknech, Stefanos Tsitsipas and 2017 champion Grigor Dimitrov.

Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry is seeded 26th. All 32 seeds receive a bye into the second round. Argentina again brought the region’s largest delegation, with eight men across the seeded and unseeded ranks. One of them has already made an impression on this swing.

Thiago Agustín Tirante beat Fritz in the Round of 64 in Montreal, an upset that cost the American the tournament he entered as a favorite and that now shadows the quarter Fritz heads in Ohio. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio is the region’s only player in the main draw. She opens against American Taylor Townsend, with the winner advancing to face world No. 2 Elena Rybakina.

It is an unforgiving path for a player who has spent the season rebuilding her ranking, though Townsend is beatable and the reward for an upset would be the highest-profile match of Osorio’s summer. Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia, listed on early entry publications, will not appear.

The former world No. 10 announced last week that she will not play again on tour this year and intends to return in 2027 using a protected ranking, after a season that produced a 4-19 record and eight consecutive losses. Four Latin American women entered qualifying instead. Argentina’s Solana Sierra went out Tuesday evening to Japan’s Aoi Ito, 6-1, 6-1, leaving Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa to chase the twelve main-draw places on offer.



In the men’s qualifying, 36-year-old Argentine Marco Trungelliti came through his opener against Sebastian Ofner in three sets, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien and Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía were still in action late Tuesday. Main-draw play begins Thursday and runs through Aug. 23, the last significant test before the US Open. For a region sending fourteen players to Ohio, the answers about form and readiness will come quickly.

World.title: The Unexpected Reason Some Travelers May Prefer Costa Rica
World.content:
My friend Tomas has worked most of his life in one kind of tourism or another. He’s 100 percent Tico but spent many years in the states and is fluent in English and wise to the ways of the bigger world. I had not heard from him in a while.

Then I got a short Whatsapp message that said: “I read your article about tourism in Central America. There was something you left out of the equation.” I called him a few hours after I saw the message.

After some small talk, he asked me if I was aware of marijuana laws throughout Central America. I admitted that I was not. It was a topic I should have anticipated as not only is Tomas a tourism expert, he is also well acquainted with the underground ganja business in Costa Rica.

He got right to the point: “Costa Rica,” he said, “will have a continual advantage because not only are our weed laws softer, so is our policing. We have medical marijuana now, and the black market also thrives. If you do have the misfortune of being stopped and searched on the street by the fuerza publica, they will usually just confiscate your stash, as long as you aren’t carrying multiple packets. What they do with your stash is anybody’s guess, but that would likely be the extent of your punishment.

“Now compare that to our neighbors. Panama has medical marijuana, but try going into a pharmacy and faking it. Probably will be an armed guard in a military uniform watching everybody who enters. Get busted even with a small amount from the street, and best case scenario they deport you. If you are not so lucky they may introduce you to one of their not so pleasant jails. You were right about them bringing in so much jack between the canal and being an international banking headquarters that more tourism is simply an added plus to the economy.

“And our neighbors to the north are even stricter. Total prohibition. Nicaragua, even recreational use is considered a serious crime. Being a tourist doesn’t help. There is no leniency. Get busted with one little joint and you will be detained and deported. Guatemala and Honduras, pretty much ditto. In Belize, you can grow your own for personal use, but otherwise buying or selling, is a crime.”

“You left out El Salvador,” I said.

“Ah yes, our new competition. I wonder how many surfers and Gen Z tourists are going to want to visit a place where not only is weed completely illegal, but the ever present security forces can search and detain you without due process. Get caught smoking a bowl and you can say goodbye to your vacation and maybe your freedom.”

“So what is your conclusion on all this?” I asked.

“The cool dictator,’ he said, referring to Bukele. “Ain’t so cool after all.”

“No. What I mean is, how is this beneficial to Costa Rica? Plenty of people can enjoy their vacation without even thinking about ganja. Millions of travelers come to Central America to enjoy the nature and the culture without a thought toward marijuana laws.”

“And millions come here hoping to score a little smoke to enhance their experience.”

“And how would you market this? What, an ad campaign showing smiling red-eyed sloths hanging from trees and puffing on spliffs?”

“Of course not. A simple, all-encompassing information campaign. There are a million ways to get these facts out to the people online. Just let them know they can light up in Costa Rica without fear of being thrown in jail with violent criminals or tossed from the country with no refunds on their hotel rooms.”

“Good luck with that,” I said.

“Luck has nothing to do with it,” he concluded. “If Costa Rica wants to continue to be the long term king of tourism in our area, all the people need to know is that we are truly the greenest destination of all.”

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 kicks off this weekend!
World.content:
Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 kicks off this weekend!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Livestock Producers Association is inviting the public to support local businesses and organizations participating in the Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 on Saturday, August 15.

The event will feature a variety of vendors offering food, drinks, agricultural products, equipment, crafts, services and other products for visitors to enjoy.

The BLPA is encouraging attendees to visit the booths, shop locally and support Belizean businesses and the agricultural community.

The Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo will take place at the National Agriculture & Trade Showgrounds in Belmopan, offering families and visitors an opportunity to enjoy a day of good food and entertainment.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture empowers Corozal farmers through Value-Adding Agro-Processing workshop
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture empowers Corozal farmers through Value-Adding Agro-Processing workshop

By Zoila Palma: The Agriculture Department in Corozal successfully hosted a comprehensive, one-day value-adding training workshop for 20 local smallholder farmers including women, men, and youth.

The workshop held on August 11, 2026, was a collaborative effort alongside the Ministry of Agriculture’s Agro-Processing Unit (led by Anna Howe and team), the Cooperatives Department (represented by Leonardo Tzib) and the Climate Resilient Agriculture Project (CRESAP, represented by Uziel Vasquez).

Topics included post-harvest losses by equipping rural communities with essential commercial food preservation skills.

Hosted for participants from Sarteneja Village—including the Sarteneja United Farmers group, Sarteneja Farmers, and the Sartenejenas Cooperative—the hands-on training resulted in the successful manufacture of four shelf-stable, high-demand products utilizing seasonal crops:

Preserved Pineapple

Carrots-Pineapple Jam

Pasta Sauce

Spicy Mango Sauce

This training is part of a broader, systemic effort by the Ministry of Agriculture to empower rural entrepreneurs, diversify income streams for small-scale farmers, and boost the tourism sector with high-quality, locally processed Belizean goods.

“By targeting long-term regional food security and agricultural resilience, the initiative ensures that women and youth are at the forefront of local economic empowerment,” the Ministry expressed.

World.title: Leader of Opposition to Prime Minister: “No means No!”
World.content:
Leader of Opposition to Prime Minister: “No means No!”

By Zoila Palma: Today, Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton issued a statement saying that the “Prime Minister and his Cabinet are now scrambling to put a square peg in a round hole. Truth be told: it can’t fit.

After months and months of calls for meaningful consultation with key stakeholders on the proposed $80 million BTL acquisition of SMART/Speednet, we are only now seeing what appears to be a veiled attempt at “consultation” after the decision has effectively been made.”

Panton said that the Opposition call “on the BTL Board of Directors to speak directly and openly with the people who ultimately have the greatest stake in this matter, the Belizean people, who are the primary owners of BTL, the workers and contributors whose monies are entrusted to the Social Security Board.”

Panton called out Prime Minister Briceno saying that he promised Belizeans the “gold standard” for transparency and accountability.

“Belizeans deserve transparency before decisions are made not explanations after the fact. On the proposed BTL/SMART acquisition, our position remains unequivocal:

NO MEANS NO.

WE SAY NO TO THE $80 MILLION BTL/SMART ACQUISITION,” Panton expressed.

World.title: Belize hosts Central American Commission for Environment and Development Technical meeting ahead of Regional Environment Ministers’ session
World.content:
Belize hosts Central American Commission for Environment and Development Technical meeting ahead of Regional Environment Ministers’ session

By Zoila Palma: Belize hosted the first technical meeting of the Central American Commission for Environment and Development (CCAD) under its Pro Tempore Presidency on August 11, 2026, as regional countries prepare for the upcoming Council of Ministers meeting. The meeting was held at the Best Western Biltmore Plaza and brought together CCAD Liaison Officers and representatives from across the region.

The meeting was chaired by Carlos Moreno of the National Biodiversity Office within the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management.

Representatives from Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama and the Dominican Republic participated in person, while Costa Rica joined virtually.

Discussions focused on preparations for the LXXV CCAD Council of Ministers Meeting scheduled for August 13.

Among the key items addressed were the agenda for the Ministers’ meeting and the Dominican Republic’s CCAD Pro Tempore Presidency Report covering January to June 2026. Participants also reviewed Belize’s priorities for its Presidency for the July to December 2026 period.

The Liaison Officers further reviewed and accepted the revised 2026-2035 CCAD Regional Environmental Strategy Framework, which is expected to guide regional environmental action over the next decade. They also reviewed and accepted the CCAD Communication Strategy and branding for the Forests of Central America and the Dominican Republic, which will be submitted to Ministers for consideration and approval.

The meeting highlights the importance of regional cooperation in addressing environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, forest protection, water security, pollution and disaster risks.

As Belize leads the CCAD Presidency during the second half of 2026, the Ministry said it remains committed to advancing Belize’s priorities, strengthening regional partnerships and contributing to solutions that benefit both communities and the environment.

World.title: Regional heads of Judiciary express concern over leaked CCJ communications
World.content:
Regional heads of Judiciary express concern over leaked CCJ communications

By Zoila Palma: The Heads of Judiciary of Barbados, The Bahamas, Belize, Guyana, the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago have issued a joint statement following recent public reports concerning internal correspondence and matters related to the administration and functioning of the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ). The statement comes amid growing scrutiny over an internal dispute at the regional court.

The judicial leaders emphasized the importance of the CCJ within the Caribbean’s legal system, noting that for countries that have accepted its appellate jurisdiction, the Court serves as their final court of appeal.

They stressed that its authority depends on “public confidence in the independence, impartiality, integrity and competence of its judges.”

The Heads of Judiciary said they would not comment on the merits of allegations attributed to individual judges or matters arising from the Court’s internal administrative and deliberative processes.

However, they expressed “grave concern about the breach of confidentiality” that led to the disclosure of what appear to be internal communications.

Despite the controversy, the regional judicial leaders reaffirmed their confidence in the CCJ as an important Caribbean institution and in the commitment of its judges to the administration of justice.

They also reaffirmed their commitment to “the independence of all regional judiciaries” and stressed the importance of maintaining public trust and confidence in courts across the region.

World.title: Cabinet to decide Speednet deal Tuesday, but Chebat says information still missing
World.content:
Cabinet to decide Speednet deal Tuesday, but Chebat says information still missing

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The BTL-Speednet acquisition is heading into its decisive week. Cabinet spent this week taking input from advocates of the deal, opponents and the regulator, and is set to take a final decision next Tuesday. Yet coming out of Cabinet, Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat acknowledged the file is not complete.

“I think they made a very comprehensive presentation but we are still waiting on some additional information before a final decision is made,” Chebat told reporters. Asked whether he was satisfied with what Cabinet heard, he noted there were three separate presentations, “all of them were good,” before repeating that additional information remains outstanding.

Pressed on whether he stands by his February position that the acquisition would not create a monopoly, Chebat offered a technical defense. “I said that in reference to the data,” he explained, adding that the current system provides for MVNOs, mobile virtual network operators, “and so that would also deal with the monopoly in terms of telecommunications.” The argument is that even with Belize’s only two network owners merged, other companies could still sell mobile service by leasing capacity on the combined network.

Asked directly whether he is prepared to decide, the minister hedged on the timeline his own Cabinet has set. “Hopefully by the time Tuesday comes around we will have enough information on which a decision could be made,” he said. And asked what exactly is lacking, Chebat declined: “No, not at this time.”

The exchange leaves the country watching a peculiar countdown. The social partners spent weeks demanding financial statements and valuation reports they say remain pending, the independent senators questioned the deal’s legality, and now the minister responsible confirms Cabinet itself is awaiting information days before its self-imposed deadline. What arrives between now and Tuesday may decide more than the vote.

World.title: Regional Judicial and Legal Services Commission responds to allegations surrounding Caribbean Court of Justice
World.content:
Regional Judicial and Legal Services Commission responds to allegations surrounding Caribbean Court of Justice

By Zoila Palma: The Regional Judicial and Legal Services Commission (RJLSC) has issued a statement addressing recent allegations concerning the administration of the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) and the independence of its judges.

The statement comes amid an internal dispute at the region’s highest court, following leaked emails in which five of the six sitting judges reportedly raised serious concerns about CCJ President Winston Anderson’s leadership, including allegations of dictatorial rule, panel-fixing and administrative overreach.

The controversy reportedly began with a unilateral proposal concerning a new judicial dress code but escalated into broader concerns about the administration of the Court, including the removal of Justice Chile Eboe-Osuji from a hearing panel.

Senior judges have reportedly warned that the dispute could threaten the independence and impartiality of the regional court.

In its August 10 statement, however, the RJLSC said it is aware of the allegations and recognizes “the seriousness of these matters and the importance of addressing them in a manner that protects public trust and confidence in the Court.”

The Commission, which was established in 2003 under the Agreement Establishing the Caribbean Court of Justice, stressed that it is an independent, non-political body responsible for appointing CCJ judges and staff, determining their terms and overseeing disciplinary action.

The RJLSC said it has operated independently for more than two decades, maintaining that its Commissioners have “enjoyed fruitful working relationships with the Court” and have functioned without interference from the Court or external actors.

The RJLSC also urged caution in drawing conclusions about the allegations before they have been properly examined. “No conclusions should be drawn about the allegations until they have been examined fairly and objectively,” the Commission stated, adding that it remains committed to its independent operations.

The Commission said it believes concerns surrounding the CCJ and RJLSC can best be addressed through established internal governance mechanisms and a transparent, independent review.
